items.title: ChatGPT in Pakistani Higher Education:  Transforming Teaching, Learning, Assessment,  Research, and Academic Ethics

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education in Pakistan has created both opportunities and concerns for educators, researchers, and policymakers. ChatGPT, a generative AI tool developed by OpenAI, can support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic work. This study examined how experienced academicians view its benefits, limitations, and ethical implications in Pakistani higher education. A qualitative exploratory design was used in this study. Twelve experienced academicians from different higher education institutions in Pakistan were selected purposively and interviewed through a semi-structured guide. The interviews were transcribed and analysed through familiarization, coding, development and review of themes. ChatGPT was used only to help organize provisional codes; the researchers checked its suggestions against the transcripts and made the final analytical decisions. Five themes were identified: teaching, learning, assessment, research, and ethics. Participants reported that ChatGPT supported lesson planning, content preparation, student engagement, idea generation, academic writing, and research productivity. They also noted that it enables students to understand difficult topics, improve their writing skills, and obtain immediate academic support. Main concerns were identified as plagiarism, over-reliance on AI-generated content, weaker critical thinking, and the absence of clear institutional policies. The findings show that ChatGPT may be useful in higher education when its use is guided by academic judgment and clear rules. Universities should redesign assessment, prepare ethical guidelines, train faculty, and strengthen AI literacy. The study offers practical information for teachers, administrators, and policymakers planning the responsible use of generative AI in Pakistan.

items.abstract_text: Why can similarly configured AI agents amplify engagement in some communities yet mainly redirect it in others? We deployed two autonomous AI agents in separate Farcaster channels (January–February 2026) across two incentive phases: Phase 1 with $Degen token rewards and Phase 2 with social recognition through agent follow-backs and mutual-follow encouragement. In /replyors (71 daily replies at baseline, Attention Saturation Ratio 1.17), the difference-in-differences (DiD)-adjusted engagement lift was [Formula: see text]228% in Phase 1 and [Formula: see text]118% in Phase 2, consistent with engagement amplification, although the seven-day baseline does not establish parallel pre-treatment trends cleanly. In /degen (244 daily replies, ASR 2.17), the channel-level DiD estimate was [Formula: see text]18% ([Formula: see text]) and not statistically distinguishable from zero despite strong topic-level participation. Because the available /degen–/base control is poorly matched on baseline scale and ASR, that comparison is treated as suggestive rather than a clean causal estimate. Phase 1 generated 967 participant reply messages from 61 unique individuals and 101,980 $Degen distributed. Using historical DEGEN/USD closes at the beginning and end of the 9–22 January reward phase as a broad valuation bracket, the aggregate token budget was on the order of US$111–152; this is not a transaction-time weighted valuation. After token removal, participant reply volume within agent-initiated threads fell by approximately 82–90% and Phase 1 participant retention was 27–34%. We introduce the Contextual Amplification Framework (CAF) and Attention Saturation Ratio (ASR) as provisional, exploratory constructs derived from two treated channels. The evidence is consistent with the possibility that pre-existing attention saturation moderates agent effects, but the ASR is not a validated screening rule and requires multi-site replication. The findings carry implications for platform economics, AI governance, and token incentive design.

items.title: <b>Roles and Research Focus of AI in Mathematics Education: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Analysis</b>

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.title: <b>AI as a New Problem Generator in the Context of Mathematical Modelling</b>

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology
items.abstract_text: Having been studied for centuries, mathematical modelling is an important perspective in mathematics education; however, teachers often face difficulties in accessing appropriate and high-quality modelling activities for classroom use. This study investigates the capacity of ChatGPT and its customised version, the Mathematical Modelling Problem Generator (MMPG), to produce mathematically and pedagogically meaningful modelling problems. Four AI-generated model-eliciting activities were comparatively analysed: three produced in independent ChatGPT-4 sessions and one produced by MMPG, all focusing on ratios and proportions. The problem scenarios were evaluated using five characteristics from established frameworks, focusing on context (non-routine and real-life relevance) and complexity (multiple steps, uncertain solution paths, and multiple solutions). The results show that ChatGPT failed to produce MEAs that met key modelling characteristics, whereas MMPG successfully generated non-routine, multi-step MEAs with unclear solution paths and multiple valid solutions. Therefore, MMPG can be considered an effective tool for supporting pedagogical practice by improving teachers’ access to and design of content-aligned, high-quality modelling activities.

items.title: Studyflow: Evidence-Informed Design and Prototyping of an AI-Assisted Academic Workload and Cognitive Support Platform for University Students Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

items.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance: Basis for AI-driven instructional toolkit

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Research Studies in Education
items.abstract_text: This study aimed to determine the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance as a basis for developing an AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit for San Carlos Elementary School, Caba, La Union. Specifically, it examined learners’ awareness and experiences in using AI tools, their level of critical thinking, academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English, and the relationship among these variables. The study employed a quantitative research design involving twenty-six (26) learner-respondents who answered a validated and reliable survey questionnaire. The findings revealed that learners had a high level of awareness of AI tools, including ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, and Jenni AI, while their learning and collaborative experiences were very high. Their overall level of critical thinking was high, with a median of 4.17, particularly in reasoning, problem-solving, and collaborative skills. Likewise, their academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English was very high, with grades ranging from 91 to 95. Statistical analysis further revealed a significant but weak positive correlation between awareness of AI tools and critical thinking (r = .300), as well as a significant positive correlation with academic performance in Mathematics (r = .343). These findings suggest that AI tools can support learners’ critical thinking and academic performance when integrated meaningfully and responsibly into instruction. The developed AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit obtained a very high level of validity, indicating its suitability for instructional use. The study recommends the guided integration of AI tools to promote responsible technology use, independent thinking, collaborative learning, and improved academic outcomes.

items.title: Bounded AI Assistance in Higher Education: Re-Aligning Pedagogy, Assessment and Institutional Governance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

items.title: BlockKD3A: A Web3-Native Framework for Decentralized Collaborative AI and User-Generated Model Assets

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
items.abstract_text: User-generated model assets in Web3 demand verifiable provenance, clear attribution, and dependable coordination across organizational boundaries without centralizing data. However, real-world deployments still face persistent challenges. Even algorithmically robust methods like KD3A often lack auditable coordination, failure resilience, and reproducible artifact lineage. These limitations make training brittle and results difficult to audit amidst node churn, adversarial behavior, and system heterogeneity. We introduce BlockKD3A, a hybrid on-chain/off-chain framework that operationalizes KD3A with three key system guarantees: (i) auditable coordination, achieved via smart contracts that record training state, model content identifiers (CIDs), and Consensus Focus (CF)-based attribution; (ii) reliability, through a transaction-safe client and failure-aware orchestration that applies nonnegative CF clipping, supports zero-CF fallback, and avoids blocking on stragglers; and (iii) reproducibility, enabled by content-addressable packaging and unified telemetry that couples machine learning metrics with blockchain events. In 9 end-to-end deployments (40 epochs per target), BlockKD3A delivered near-centralized performance, 96.74% macro-average accuracy on Office-Caltech10, and 89.40% on DigitFive—substantially outperforming representative federated baselines. Coordination remained efficient and predictable, with only 13 blockchain transactions across all 9 deployments, bounded gas costs per write (125,972–298,405), and stable epoch timings even under partial participation. By integrating KD3A’s algorithm-native attribution with on-chain provenance and robust execution, BlockKD3A closes the gap between decentralized learning algorithms and reliable system deployment, providing auditability, predictable cost envelopes, and transferable engineering patterns for verifiable user-generated model assets.

items.abstract_text: This paper reports on a qualitative study with 12 experts across dermatology and radiology about the risk of AI-induced skill erosion. Integrating AI tools (e.g., visual diagnosis, generative scribes) into medical workflows introduces the risk of AI-induced skill erosion among experts despite short-term efficiency gains. While existing literature focuses on short-term behavioral phenomena like automation bias and real-time accuracy, it fails to capture how continuous AI integration alters what clinicians consider essential skills and reshapes professional identity over time. We conducted 12 semi-structured interviews and speculative design workbook activities with expert radiologists and dermatologists. From this study, we derived the Human-AI Clinical Skill Framework, which maps how modular, unitary, and dynamic skill philosophies intersect with mechanical, integrative, and translational skill tiers, and what it means for clinical expertise in an AI-powered practice. We conclude with design principles for integrating AI into medical tools to mitigate skill erosion.

analysis.methods: To answer our research question, we conducted a qualitative empirical study combining semi-structured interviews with speculative design workbook activities. We selected dermatology and radiology as our primary contexts because both domains involved imaging-based pattern recognition, making them early adopters of AI-powered diagnostic systems. This approach lets us ground the study in present workflows while pushing participants beyond current technology limitations to pinpoint their comfort boundaries, mental models, and professional values around AI integration [10] . We recruited 12 medical professionals (6 dermatologists and 6 radiologists) through purposeful sampling and professional network snowballing. Inclusion criteria required participants to be at least 19 years old, hold an active medical license or residency appointment in dermatology or radiology, and actively engage in imaging-based diagnosis as part of their routine practice.The participant pool was balanced across career stages, ranging from trainees/residents to senior professors, across six countries (Australia, USA, Canada, Germany, Italy, UK), offering diverse views on training systems and professional code of conduct. Participant familiarity with AI was categorized qualitatively based on self-reported clinical and research experience, spanning a spectrum from daily clinical use of commercial software to trial-or research-only exposure influenced by differing national regulatory frameworks. Data collection was structured into two parts, conducted remotely in one 60-minute session. Both parts were conducted individually. Part 1-Semi-structured interview: This part explored realworld clinical workflows, time distribution, and mental effort across tasks. To ground reflections in lived practice rather than abstract speculation, participants walked through recent standard versus complex diagnostic cases (e.g., "Which parts feel most meaningful or professionally satisfying?"). We probed participants' explicit conceptions of clinical competence (e.g., "How do you tell if someone is a good dermatologist/radiologist?") and the factors governing accountability and error management in imaging workflows (e.g., "What is the consequence you would face for missing or providing an incorrect diagnosis?"). For participants with prior exposure to clinical AI decision support, we explored how these tools impacted their performance and perceived skill trajectories. Part 2-Speculative design workbook activities: Participants engaged in a two-part speculative design activity designed to push their boundaries around AI task delegation and evaluate how different interface interactions shape cognitive engagement: (1) Compare-and-contrast interaction paradigms: Participants were introduced to two contrasting diagnostic interface paradigms. The Recommendation-First layout immediately presents AI predictions, confidence scores, and suggested clinical actions upon opening a study. The Cognition-First layout requires the clinician to input their independent diagnosis first before revealing AI assessments. Participants discussed suitable tasks, required operator skills, and performance thresholds for each interaction mode. (2) Boundary-finding scenarios: We presented three scenarios, and asked participants to reflect on how these scenarios align with their values, cognitive process, and responsibilities, and how delegation to extreme use of AI in different parts of the work may affect their skills and professional code of conduct. The scenarios were: • Case filtering based on AI's diagnosis confidence: AI independently flags and filters high-confidence cases (e.g., >95% confidence) so they never reach human expert eyes, though humans can audit. This scenario focuses on autonomy, accountability, and authority. • Autonomous biopsy scheduling: AI automatically schedules biopsies, generates pre-operative instructions, and updates system records upon detecting high-risk conditions, leaving clinicians to override asynchronously. This scenario focuses on accountability, workload, and integration into workflow. • AI-generated referrals: AI automatically generates and sends referral letters to specialist departments (e.g., Oncology) or back to the general physician following human-AI joint diagnosis, with the clinician CC'ed. This scenario focuses on professional communication and reputation. Audio recordings were transcribed verbatim and analyzed following an inductive-to-deductive thematic analysis approach [2] . • Inductive Analysis: The primary researcher performed invivo open coding on raw transcripts to preserve natural clinical vocabulary surrounding workflow, cognitive burden, and identity. Through regular iterative team debriefs, initial codes were grouped into broader thematic clusters reflecting clinical skill types and delegation attitudes. From these clusters, we derived the core 3×3 matrix structuring our framework. • Deductive Analysis: The research team applied a deductive coding pass to populate the matrix cells across all transcripts. Crucially, our analysis revealed that the three skill philosophies (modular, unitary, dynamic) do not represent rigid, mutually exclusive clinician personality types. Rather, an individual clinician may adopt fluid philosophical positions depending on task context, risk tier, or professional role. For instance, participants frequently held a Unitary stance when supervising trainees or evaluating high-stakes diagnostic edge cases-insisting on unassisted human reasoning-yet shifted toward a Modular or Dynamic stance when executing routine administrative tasks or personal high-volume screening.
analysis.discussion: The workplace dynamics identified in this study connect directly to established empirical work on clinical AI adoption. Prior research has documented how AI integration into the medical workflow can threaten professional identity [11] , the necessity of redesigning curricula alongside AI integration [14] , and the concern around automation bias for clinician's decision support [1] . Our Human-AI Clinical Skill framework builds upon these isolated observations by providing a unified conceptual framework. By mapping these phenomena across skill philosophies and skill tiers, we offer a structured foundation for future research on cognitive skill erosion and clinical workflow design. Our framework also refines and extends existing AI implementation frameworks in medicine. While scoping reviews emphasize organizational adaptation and technical translation [7] , our work focuses on the underlying clinician's skill philosophies and how they influence the opportunities and potential pitfalls at different skill tiers. Design frameworks establishing requirements for trustworthy healthcare AI [18] are extended by looking at AI in tasks beyond diagnosis and imagining AI support under the shifting role of healthcare providers. Finally, our framework adds to the discussion around the legal framework for AI adoption [19] by surfacing the common patterns across clinicians in various locations around the world on what constitutes clinical accountability and core competencies. Based on our framework, we outline three design principles for AIintegrated clinical tools to mitigate skill erosion, support evolving medical roles, and align with clinicians' underlying skill philosophies: (1) Enable specialization transitions (addressing 4.3.1 & 4.4): As diagnostic tasks migrate to AI, systems should equip emerging specializations (e.g., technical auditor, interpersonal communicators) with the target metrics they need to guide their evolving workflow. For instance, technical auditors' interfaces should provide visibility into the model's training and analysis for accurate identification of risks and errors. As for patient communication, systems should provide visual risk translation tools, such as patient-facing vocabularies and diagrams, to help bridge the comprehension gap between complex model outputs and actionable patient dialogue. (2) Prevent automation bias (addressing 4.2): Interfaces should enforce independent clinician reasoning before displaying machine predictions to ensure that its decision is taken strictly as a "second opinion". This approach is called cognitionfirst in human-AI interaction literature and could be executed through various mechanisms, such as evaluative AI [13] and frictional AI [16] . It introduces the Human-AI Clinical Skill framework, which connects three clinical skill tiers (mechanical, integrative, and translational) with three skill philosophies (modular, unitary, and dynamic). Our findings reveal that clinicians do not perceive skill erosion as an inevitable consequence of AI integration, but risks occur when tasks are segmented and delegated under acute workload pressure, leading to lack of foundational intuition in trainees and passive AI oversight in experts. Beyond interface design, this work also offers novel considerations and challenges on how medical codes of conduct and legal liability frameworks should adapt as human expertise evolves in the AI-assisted healthcare workflow.

items.title: Impact of Perceived AI Threat on Unemployment Anxiety and Psychological Well-Being among IT Employees

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.

analysis.discussion: The research investigated how perceived threat from artificial intelligence (AI) correlates with unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being of employees in the IT industry. The results showed that there is a positive correlation between perceived threat from AI and unemployment anxiety. It turns out that people who see the threat of losing their job to AI experience more anxiety about it. Moreover, the findings demonstrated that perceived threat from AI is negatively correlated with psychological well-being. Therefore, higher threat perception results in lower psychological well-being. On the other hand, the correlation analysis indicates that unemployment anxiety is not related to psychological well-being. Therefore, it can be concluded that perceived threat from AI is one of the main psychological issues of employees whose work The positive association of the perceived AI threat with anxiety over unemployment follows the ideas laid out in the STARA awareness model developed by Brougham and Haar (2018), where employees' worries related to intelligent technologies and AI in general can result in negative job- and wellness-related effects. As AI systems take over the tasks previously performed by people, workers may become more anxious about the prospects of their jobs and employment as a whole. The current discovery implies that those employees who believe there is a higher chance of AI replacing them are also more anxious about unemployment. This finding also coincides with the job insecurity theories, which describe job insecurity as the feeling of uncertainty regarding possible job loss (Greenhalgh & Rosenblatt, 1984; Sverke et al., 2002). Therefore, the idea of being replaced by AI can be an important factor influencing job insecurity even in those cases when an employee remains employed. The fact that there is a negative link between the perceived AI threats and psychological well- being highlights the idea that problems associated with technological efficacy affect the psychological state of workers. Brougham and Haar (2018) noted that having the relevant knowledge about STARA had an impact on career satisfaction and well-being parameters of employees. Ryff (1989) described psychological well-being as something that involves functionality in terms of having autonomy, personal development, mastery of the environment, goals in life, and positivity in relationships. The worries about the job replacement and prospects of getting a job in the future possibly decrease the perceived controllability, safety, and meaning of life of individuals. The negative links in this case can indicate that people experience psychological discomfort due to technological uncertainties. It is curious that anxiety over unemployment showed no statistically significant correlation with psychological well-being in the correlation analysis. This suggests that while employees’ perceptions of the threat of AI were linked with increased anxiety over unemployment as well as decreased psychological well-being, anxiety over unemployment itself did not correlate significantly with psychological well-being. The present pattern implies that the threat of AI may involve wider issues related to technological change, professional identity, skills and career prospects that may affect psychological well-being regardless of unemployment anxiety. Prior studies have argued that there is a difference between cognitive perceptions of job insecurity and emotional reaction to insecurity, thus suggesting that the two can lead to distinct psychological consequences (Jiang & Lavaysse, 2018). However, this interpretation should be treated with caution and needs further elaboration using advanced analytical techniques and proper measures In short, this research contributes to existing studies on AI-related employment issues, because it combines in a single investigation perceived threat of AI technology, anxiety regarding job loss and psychological well-being of IT specialists. The existing body of studies reveals the worries of employees in relation to the possibility of technological substitution and confirms the association of awareness of STARA with other aspects in the workplace and well-being (Brougham & Haar, 2018). The literature related to job insecurity points to the significance of perception of job insecurity by employees for their mental and professional functioning (Sverke et al., 2002). The current study undertakes the analysis of the relationship between perceived threat of AI and job loss anxiety and psychological well-being of the employees in Pakistan. The results of the current study show the significance of organizational actions aimed at creating conditions under which it is easier for employees to deal with their concerns about the future job The current study investigated the connection between the perception of AI threat, unemployment anxiety, and psychological well-being among IT workers. It has been found out that the perception of AI threat was positively connected with unemployment anxiety and negatively connected with psychological well-being, but the association between unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being was insignificant during the correlation analysis. This means that perceptions of employees about the AI-related employment threats may have an impact on psychological experiences and may be related to the issues concerning future employment and well-being of employees. It can be seen that the psychological experience of employees should be considered in addition to the advancement of technology. The organization may gain certain benefits through the creation of an opportunity for the development of skills, communication, and adaptation of employees to AI-related changes in work.
analysis.limitations: The current research presents several limitations which ought to be taken into consideration while interpreting the results. First of all, the cross-sectional correlational method is incapable of establishing causal conclusions concerning the relationship between perceived AI threat, unemployment anxiety, and psychological well-being. Although a significant relationship has been found, the question of whether the participants see AI as a threat to their job due to their unemployment anxiety or people are anxious about losing their jobs because they are low in psychological well-being cannot be answered. Secondly, the research utilized a convenience sample, which might limit the representativity of the sample and extent to which the results can be generalized across IT population. The sample consisted of 150 respondents whereby the majority were male aged between 20-40. Furthermore, it can be seen that the respondents belong to the private sector which makes the application of the results on employees from other sectors less feasible. Third, all variables were measured using self-report methods. Thus, answers could have been subject to respondents' interpretations of the questionnaire items and influenced by social desirability and various response tendencies. Apparently, application of the self-report measurement tool for all variables also creates the chance for prevalence of common method Fourth, the measurement of unemployment anxiety needs to be clarified in regards to its origins and construct validation. It is noted that the measure in the study includes seven questions and has good internal consistency, but its original authorship, psychometric properties, and precise assessment of unemployment anxiety should be confirmed. Furthermore, the psychological well- being measure must be defined to ensure the relevance of the measure used and obtained results. Finally, the study was limited by the specific occupational and national context. The employees of the IT sector can experience different exposure to AI technologies and concerns about employment as compared to workers in other fields. Therefore, the results may not be fully generalizable to other occupations and countries. Further research on the topic should focus on using longitudinal or multiple wave research designs in order to study how the constructs of perceived AI threat, employment anxiety, and psychological well-being may be influenced over time by the exposure of the workers to AI technologies in their work environment. Probability-based sampling method, where possible, and increased sample sizes from both public and private sector organizations should be employed in future studies on the topic. Increased gender, age, education, and experience heterogeneity of the samples studied would contribute to the generalizability of results obtained. Comparison of employees working in IT and non-IT professions could uncover whether the direct contact with AI technology results in specific psychological concerns for the employees. In future research, one might also look at other constructs like self-efficacy regarding AI, perceived organizational support, job insecurity, career adaptability, technological skills, and coping to determine the reasons for increased levels of psychological issues experienced by workers due to changes resulting from the use of AI in the workplace. Lastly, future research can be conducted on organizational interventions, including training related to AI, career development, supportive leadership, and open communication on AI. items.title: AI-Based Social Connection Interventions of Emerging Categories of Support for Older Adults: Scoping Review

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Social connection is a critical determinant of well-being in later life. However, older adults often experience social isolation and increased loneliness, which are associated with mental and physical health challenges. AI-based interventions have emerged as scalable approaches to support social connection. A growing body of research has examined the effects of individual AI technologies on improving social connection across diverse devices and care settings. Despite growing evidence of their effects, little attention has been paid to the common pathways through which these interventions support social connection. Objective This scoping review aimed to develop a typology of common categories of support across AI-based interventions and to map how these categories are configured in different intervention contexts. Methods Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published from 2016 through 2025. Studies were included if they examined AI-based interventions designed to support social connection among older adults, conceptualized as a multidimensional construct encompassing loneliness reduction, social interaction, and behavioral engagement. Results A total of 1110 articles were retrieved, of which 47 met the inclusion criteria. Qualitative and mixed methods studies were the most prevalent (n=32, 68%), with quantitative studies accounting for the remainder (n=15, 32%). Four common support categories were identified: relational interaction (forming ties), emotional support (enhancing interaction quality), functional support (sustaining engagement), and risk detection (reducing constraints). Relational interaction and emotional support were present across all studies. Functional support and risk detection were observed in 70% (n=33) and 17% (n=8) of studies, respectively. The most prevalent configuration combined relational interaction, emotional support, and functional support, forming a companionship-plus-routine pathway that sustained engagement in everyday contexts. Functional support was associated with sustained participation in daily routines and activities, which may have contributed to opportunities for ongoing social interaction. Risk detection, while less prevalent, functioned as a constraint-reducing condition that supported continuity of engagement. Conclusions This review proposes a conceptual framework that shifts attention from specific technologies to the interactional configurations that enable AI to support social connection across care settings. This framework may inform the design and tailoring of AI-based interventions to address the multidimensional nature of social connection among older adults.

items.abstract_text: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

items.title: The impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on employee green well-being: The mediating role of employee engagement in Vietnamese enterprises

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
items.abstract_text: Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

analysis.methods: The target population consists of full-time employees of organizations in Vietnam that have incorporated Generative AI into their daily operations, spanning information technology, finance–banking, media, and retail. Respondents were reached through three categorized source channels aligned with the sampling criteria: (i) alumni and professional networks of the authors’ universities, primarily reaching knowledge workers in information technology and finance– banking enterprises; (ii) human resource focal points in AI-adopting enterprises in Ho Chi Minh City and neighboring provinces, covering media/marketing and retail/e-commerce firms; and (iii) professional online communities of Generative AI users in Vietnam, through which additional snowball referrals were generated. Across these three channels combined, a total of 412 questionnaires were distributed between December 2025 and March 2026 via an online survey (Google Forms). Screening questions at the start of the questionnaire verified three eligibility criteria: (1) full-time employment status; (2) use of Generative AI at least once per week for a minimum of three months; and (3) voluntary informed consent to participate. Of the 412 questionnaires distributed, 389 were returned; after excluding 47 invalid responses (straight-lining, internally inconsistent answers, or excessive missing data), the final sample comprised 342 valid responses (effective response rate = 83.0%). The sectoral composition of the final sample (Table 1) reflects the coverage of these three channels, with information technology (32.7%) and finance –banking (23.1%) accounting for the largest shares [ 30] . The adequacy of the sample size was established using two complementary criteria. First, under the ten-times rule of Thu et al / OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development, 19:11,2026 101 thumb, the minimum sample equals ten times the largest number of structural paths directed at any single construct in the model - three paths (POS_ATT, RAIS, and ENG) pointing at each well-being dimension when direct effects are estimated for mediation testing - yielding a minimum of 30 observations [30]. Second, and more rigorously, the inverse square root method [31] was applied: assuming a conservatively small minimum path coefficient of 0.20, a 5% significance level, and 80% statistical power, the required minimum sample is approximately 155 respondents. The final sample of 342 exceeds both thresholds by a comfortable margin and also surpasses the level of 200 observations commonly regarded as sufficient for stable PLS-SEM estimation, thereby ensuring adequate statistical power for testing the hypothesized structural and mediation effects. All constructs were measured using a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5 = strongly agree). Positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT, 4 items) were adapted from [ 12] and [23] to fit the Generative AI context. Responsible AI signals (RAIS, 5 items) capture transparency, explainability, and fairness, based on [ 18-20]. Employee engagement (ENG, 9 items) was measured using the UWES-9 scale developed by [ 24] , encompassing three dimensions: vigor, dedication, and absorption. Green emotional eell- being (GEW, 4 items) was adapted from [ 6]; green cognitive well- being (GCW, 4 items) from [7]; and green social well- being (GSW, 4 items) from [ 8]. The survey instrument was developed in Vietnamese using a back-translation procedure to ensure linguistic equivalence. analysis.discussion: The results support H1 with high statistical significance (β = 0.312, t = 5.847, p < 0.001) and a small-to-medium effect size (f² = 0 .128 [30]), indicating that positive attitudes toward AI play a meaningful role in fostering engagement. This finding is consistent with prior research while extending its explanatory scope. Specifically, [ 10] demonstrated that POS_ATT promotes GenAI usage behavior (β = 0.372), whereas the present results advance this line of inquiry by showing that positive attitudes not only influence behavior but also directly activate a deeper psychological state - namely, engagement. The comparatively lower effect size may reflect the Vietnamese context, where familiarity with AI remains limited, thereby attenuating the conversion intensity from attitude to psychological state. Relative to [25], this study adds evidence that not only AI efficacy but also cognitive attitudes (POS_ATT) constitute independent antecedents of engagement, suggesting that cognitive resources and individual capability operate in parallel in activating engagement within AI -integrated work environments. The findings further complement [ 11] by demonstrating that engagement need not be a downstream consequence of well-being alone; it can equally be initiated by prior cognitive attitudes, implying the potential existence of a reciprocal relationship between these constructs. Theoretically, this finding aligns with JD-R Theory, under which positive attitudes toward AI may be conceptualized as a cognitive job resource that activates the motivational process and fosters engagement through the satisfaction of autonomy and competence needs [14] . In the Vietnamese context, where awareness of AI's role in professional development is growing, this mechanism becomes particularly salient, creating conditions under which POS_ATT is progressively converted into sustained engagement. The results support H2 with statistical significance (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) and a small-to-medium effect size (f² =0 .108), marginally lower than that observed for H1. This suggests that responsible AI signals exert a meaningful influence on engagement, albeit through a more indirect and less immediate mechanism than positive cognitive attitudes. This finding is consistent with [ 20] , a foundational study grounded in Signal Mechanism Outcome Theory, in which responsible AI signals- including transparency, fairness, and explainability- each positively predicted engagement. The present study, however, extends this work in three directions: (i) by integrating RAIS into the JD-R framework, thereby establishing an explicit theoretical link to the resource-based mechanism; (ii) by testing the relationship in a multi- industry enterprise context rather than the healthcare sector; and (iii) by modeling RAIS as a second- order construct rather than a set of discrete signals. Relative to [ 4], the current findings offer more direct evidence by operationalizing engagement in its psychological sense using the UWES, rather than relying solely on behavioral intention measures. The study further complements [26] by clarifying the mediating mechanism: rather than operating directly, RAIS influences well-being through engagement as the intervening psychological pathway. Theoretically, the results can be interpreted through the dual lens of JD-R Theory and information asymmetry. The inherent opacity of AI systems generates cognitive anxiety and depletes psychological resources among employees. In this context, RAIS functions as a job resource that reduces uncertainty, reinforces trust, and liberates cognitive capacity, thereby activating engagement [14]. The comparatively lower effect size relative to H1 may reflect the Vietnamese context, where awareness of and institutional frameworks for responsible AI practices remain nascent. Consequently, while RAIS carries significant theoretical and practical relevance, its influence on engagement has yet to match the motivational potency of direct cognitive factors such as positive attitudes toward AI. The results strongly support H3a through H3c, with engagement positively predicting all three dimensions of Green Thu et al / OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development, 19:11,2026 107 Well-being: emotional (β = 0.441, f² = 0.242), cognitive (β = 0.418, f² = 0.211), and social (β = 0.397, f² = 0.189), all at p <0.001. The effect sizes range from medium to large, affirming the central role of engagement in generating green well- being. These findings are consistent with JD -R Theory at the outcome level, whereby engagement serves as the pivotal mechanism through which job resources are converted into positive individual outcomes. Compared with [ 10] , the present study demonstrates that the effect of engagement on emotional well-being (β =0.441) substantially exceeds the direct effect of GenAI usage on well-being (β = .199), reinforcing the argument that individual psychological mechanisms operating through engagement carry greater explanatory power than purely social mechanisms such as team cohesion. With respect to cognitive well-being, the results align with [17] while extending the evidence base by explicitly disaggregating the cognitive dimension, revealing that engagement not only improves affective states but also promotes competence development and sense of mastery over work. This is particularly consequential in AI-integrated environments, where engagement may generate a positive feedback loop between work experience and technological capability. Relative to [ 36] , this study broadens the role of engagement from a mediating variable to a direct predictor of multidimensional well- being, consistent with the theoretical position that engagement simultaneously constitutes an outcome of job resources and a resource that produces subsequent positive outcomes [ 2]. Notably, the descending pattern of effect sizes- GEW -> GCW - > GSW - warrants attention. analysis.limitations: Several limitations warrant acknowledgement. First, the cross-sectional design constrains causal inference. Although the POS_ATT/RAIS → ENG → Green Well -being model is grounded in established theory, the possibility of reciprocal relationships - particularly between well-being and engagement - cannot be excluded [ 11]. Second, convenience and snowball sampling concentrated in major urban centers, with a disproportionate representation of technology and finance sectors, limits generalizability. Consequently, the findings primarily reflect knowledge workers with high AI usage rates rather than the broader workforce. Finally , the risk of common method bias persists given single-source self-reported data, although statistical tests indicated an acceptable level [ 35]. These findings raise several questions that warrant further investigation. First, longitudinal or cross-lagged designs are needed to establish whether POS_ATT and RAIS lead to subsequent changes in engagement and Green Well-being, or whether reciprocal relationships exist whereby employees with higher well-being subsequently become more engaged and develop more favorable perceptions of AI. Second, future studies should investigate boundary conditions—including AI literacy, technostress, job autonomy, task c haracteristics, organizational AI culture, and intensity of AI use—to explain when the proposed pathways become stronger or weaker. Third, the comparatively weaker ENG–GSW relationship warrants greater attention to team-level mechanisms such as human–AI collaboration, team cohesion, social support, and changes in coworker interaction. Fourth, future research could extend RAIS beyond transparency, explainability, and justice to examine autonomy and non- maleficence and determine whether different responsible-AI signals produce distinct employee outcomes. items.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

reading.overview: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while.
reading.interpretation: GenAI has not simply added one more tool to the educator's kit; it has unsettled the very hierarchies that underwrote models like Bloom's Taxonomy. By revising, inverting, or 'UnBlooming' those models, the approaches in this article argue for designs that foreground recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth as the real work of learning, especially in an age where GenAI is marketed as doing the 'thinking' for us. The future of learning is not arriving later. It is already here, unevenly distributed across classrooms, disciplines, and institutions. Designing for recursion, reflection, and metacognitive growth means little if only a subset of students and faculty have the material and institutional support to engage in that work. GenAI cannot be framed primarily as a compliance or efficiency problem because it is a fundamental change in the way teaching and learning happen. Taken together, these post-AI frameworks reframe Bloom's Taxonomy not as a ladder to be climbed, but as a historical starting point-inviting educators to design learning that prioritizes metacognition, agency, and ethical judgment in a world where answers are instant but understanding is not. This does not mean being a full-on AI adopter, but it does mean that they will need to be 'AI aware' (Watkins 2024) . In comparing selected pre-AI and post-AI pedagogical frameworks according to how they conceptualize the relationship among process, product, cognition, agency, and metacognitive reflection, we have demonstrated how learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks can be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning. items.abstract_text: In spite of the fact that there is widespread agreement regarding the ethical principles that need to guide artificial intelligence, there is still a significant gap between these normative objectives and the operational realities of technical implementation. An investigation into how to operationalize a proactive, iterative AI governance paradigm is the focus of this study. The investigation is conducted via the prism of private law liabilities and constant technical verification. Both corporate compliance theater and opportunistic ethics shopping are the driving forces behind our inquiry. Both of these shortcomings in practice have occurred repeatedly. During the course of the study, a multi-layered methodological framework is utilized. This framework triangulates a comparative assessment of growing international regulatory frameworks and a "cross-sectoral typological mapping of auditing procedures from banking, data privacy, and environmental law." The findings reveal a systemic disconnect: corporate ethical commitments continue to be largely detached from operational audit systems, leaving data scientists frustrated by guidelines that are too abstract to act on. Furthermore, existing environmental, social, and governance standards do not provide any AI-specific tools for quantifying the hidden socio-technical harms that are embedded in global supply chains. rules that are abstract, whereas the existing ESG standards do not provide the AI-specific guidance that is required to assess the hidden socio-technical damages that are present throughout global supply chains.The purpose of this article is to offer a solution to this problem by advocating for the transition from voluntary soft law to an enforceable, longitudinal regulatory framework. We propose that corporate governance frameworks be merged with automated auditing pipelines, value-based engineering (also known as ethics-by-design), and independent third-party oversight. This would result in the transformation of abstract ethical concepts into private law duties that can be verified.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC GLOBAL VALUE CHAINS AND HIGHER EDUCATION TRANSFORMATION: RE-ENGINEERING INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS PEDAGOGY IN THE ERA OF AUTONOMOUS INTELLIGENCE

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

items.title: AI Marketing Transparency and Brand Trust: How AI Literacy and Perceived Manipulative Intent Shape Consumer Responses in Pakistan

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: With AI’s increasing role in digital marketing, a brand’s transparency about its use of AI could act as an informational signal of accountability. However, the interpretation consumers make of such transparency might vary with their knowledge of AI and their perception of persuasive intent. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI marketing transparency, brand trust, and purchase intention and the role of perceived manipulative intent as a mechanism and AI literacy as a boundary condition. We surveyed 387 matched Pakistani consumers, in two waves. AI literacy was operationalised with the core 18-item AI literacy dimensions of the MAILS instrument (use and apply AI, know and understand AI, detect AI, and AI ethics), whereas the remaining MAILS dimensions were treated as separate constructs. We tested the hypotheses using regression-based simple mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and first-stage moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 7). Perceived AI marketing transparency was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Brand trust carried a significant indirect association between perceived AI marketing transparency and purchase intention (indirect effect = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.11]); the direct association was not statistically significant (c′ = 0.10, p = 0.081). Perceived manipulative intent was negatively associated with brand trust (b = −0.25, p < 0.001). AI literacy positively moderated the association between perceived AI marketing transparency and perceived manipulative intent (B = 0.13, p = 0.031), such that this association was positive and significant only at high AI literacy (B = 0.25, p < 0.001). The conditional indirect association was statistically distinguishable from zero only at high AI literacy (effect = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.13, −0.01]). The index of moderated mediation was statistically significant at the 5% level (index = −0.03, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.001]) but the CI was close to the null value. The results are consistent with both theoretically opposite mechanisms suggested: an accountability-related association between perceived transparency and brand trust, and a conditional suspicion-related indirect association via perceived manipulative intent, which were analysed under the umbrella of two different empirical models. The interaction was small and the moderated-mediation evidence was statistically weak and should be considered a preliminary rather than a general finding of the negative effects on transparency. One of the contributions of the study is distinguishing perceived transparency from its interpretation, and examining core AI literacy competencies in addition to a focused measure of persuasion knowledge activation in the context of AI marketing and signaling research. Finally, practical implications highlight the importance of AI disclosure being credible and context-specific, not necessarily a strategy that builds trust.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Clinical prediction models have historically relied on structured electronic health record data, leaving the rich prognostic signal embedded in free-text clinical documentation systematically underutilized. The proposed Clinical Multimodal Adaptive Clinical Prediction (CMACP) architecture — a dual-pathway prediction system integrating structured EHR features through gradient-boosted tree processing with unstructured clinical note embeddings through Clinical BERT encoding, unified by a cross-modal attention mechanism that weighs each modality's contribution by predictive confidence. The architecture is designed for geriatric acute care settings where clinical notes capture disease severity, symptom trajectory, and functional context unavailable from structured data alone. A federated fine-tuning protocol enables privacypreserving multi-institutional model development across health systems with different EHR platforms and patient populations. An attribution framework combining SHAP-based structured feature importance with Integrated Gradients note concept attribution provides role-differentiated clinical explanations, with a concordance quality badge signalling modality alignment. A governance framework specifies deployment standards, post-market performance monitoring, and equity evaluation protocols calibrated to multi-site clinical NLP systems. The CMACP framework addresses the technical and governance requirements for safe deployment of multimodal clinical AI in settings where older adult patients are most vulnerable to prediction errors. External validation across multiple health system types, equity stratification by race and documentation quality environment, and prospective evaluation of attribution quality are identified as priority research requirements.

items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

The readerly distraction model developed here distinguishes justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently connected to the disclosed operation or its plausible epistemic consequences. Such monitoring may redirect attention away from a manuscript's claims, evidence, and reasoning, and under some conditions may contribute to negative perceptions of authorial competence, originality, or trustworthiness. However, attentional displacement and evaluative stigma remain analytically distinct. Their relationship is an empirical question that can be examined through comparisons of function-specific disclosures, generic disclosures, and equivalent forms of human mediation. The appropriate policy response is epistemically proportionate reporting rather than either exhaustive provenance reconstruction or the abandonment of disclosure. Methodological reporting should make consequential research operations examinable; governance reporting should identify how adopted outputs were assessed and controlled; and production-provenance disclosure should communicate relevant circumstances of composition without claiming to reconstruct every intellectual influence. Authorship, in turn, cannot rest on nominal responsibility alone. Accountable judgment requires understanding, appropriate verification, meaningful decision authority, and answerability that can be exercised when justified challenges arise. These capacities cannot be certified infallibly, nor must every contributor personally reproduce every specialized procedure in collaborative research. Nevertheless, claims about responsible authorship can be examined through role-specific explanations, relevant verification records, and substantive responses to criticism. The distinction is between responsibility merely attributed to an author and judgment that can be meaningfully questioned and defended. The central ethical task is therefore not to determine what proportion of a manuscript originated with AI, but to establish what information is necessary for evaluating its claims and who can justify the scholarly decisions embodied in them. A defensible publication policy should make consequential operations visible without allowing technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning. items.abstract_text: Purpose As biodiversity governance becomes increasingly important for sustainable development, understanding how government-generated intangible knowledge influences financial decision-making remains an underexplored issue in intellectual capital (IC) research. Drawing on IC theory, this study conceptualizes government biodiversity attention (GBA) as institutional environmental intelligence and examines its effect on high-carbon loans (HCL). Design/methodology/approach This study constructs a novel GBA index using machine learning and text analysis of 5,726 Chinese local government work reports from 2003–2023. Using a panel dataset of 287 Chinese commercial banks from 2016–2023, this study employs fixed-effects regression models, instrumental variable estimation, propensity score matching (PSM), and placebo tests to examine how GBA influences HCL. Findings GBA is significantly negatively associated with HCL by financial institutions. This effect is more pronounced in cities with well-developed green finance systems and low-carbon pilot policies, among local commercial banks and banks actively engaged in green credit practices. Further channel analyses indicate that the relationship between GBA and HCL is associated with environmental constraints, capital adequacy, and bank risk-taking. Originality/value This study develops a novel machine learning-based measure of GBA and provides empirical evidence of how this institutional environmental intelligence influences HCL. It extends the IC perspective to government-generated intangible knowledge, showing how such knowledge shapes financial institutions' environmental cognition and sustainable credit allocation.

items.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
items.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.
