Existing interventions typically lack real-time responsiveness and ecological validity. This study retrospectively examined historical training records from an AI-assisted closed-loop system integrating emotion recognition and behavioral feedback for attention regulation in children with ADHD. Methods: This single-center retrospective analysis included historical training records from 60 children with ADHD who had completed either AI-assisted attention training or conventional attention training between 2021 and 2024. The AI-assisted training-record group comprised children whose archived records included 12 sessions of integrated cognitive training involving Go/No-Go, CPT, and Flanker tasks with real-time AI-generated feedback based on task performance and facial-emotion monitoring. The conventional training-record group completed the same attention tasks without AI-based feedback. Assessments included task performance, Conners Continuous Performance Test, 3rd Edition (CPT-3), teacher ratings, and emotion metrics, analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, linear growth modeling, and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: Compared with conventional training records, AI-assisted training records showed greater pre-post changes in reaction time (RT), RT variability, and task accuracy, together with fewer commission errors in CPT-3. Post-feedback behavioral recovery was observed in 78.3% of feedback events. Teacher ratings showed consistent pre-post improvements across attention maintenance, emotional regulation, and task execution. Negative emotion labels decreased from 42.3% to 24.6% (p = 0.003). SEM supported an associative pathway linking emotion recognition frequency, feedback frequency, and RT reduction (95% CI: 0.15-0.38). Conclusions: The retrospective findings suggest that AI-assisted closed-loop training records were associated with favorable changes in attention and emotional-state indicators in children with ADHD. These exploratory results support further prospective, externally validated studies before broader clinical or educational implementation.

items.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

items.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
items.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

Moreover, PRs can be rejected; thus, it is also challenging to discern expert contributions among PRs accepted and not [79] . Hence, we investigate developer motivation, analyzing the single commits from the projects analyzed in the reference study [65] with a broader selection of product and process metrics. Furthermore, developers' commits, PRs, and code comments may not be able to capture all the motivations pushing developers to refactor the codebase; hence, we ask the following: Are there additional motivations driving the developers' willingness to perform refactoring? Refactoring improves source code quality [50] ; yet, quality improvements in readability, performance, safety, and security are only part of the overall picture [48] . For instance, in an industrial context, it is essential to assess refactoring opportunities in situations with limited resources regarding work allocation and time [71] . Silva et al. [65] succeeded in identifying 44 refactoring RMs at the time they ran their study. Therefore, we investigate whether external limitations or additional motivations influence refactoring efforts. Based on Pantiuchina et al. [49] , a relationship exists between specific quality metrics and refactoring operations. analysis.discussion: We leverage the following section to discuss the key findings of our study by relating the outcomes to every research question and identifying actionable implications for researchers and practitioners. We also address the applicability of our results in favour of refactoring recommendation systems. As shown in RQ 1 , LLMs agreed with human judgments in 80% of the cases but only 47% matched RMs from the reference study. Systematic disagreements emerged, as confirmed by Bowker's test, with LLMs tending to interpret RMs based on local code cues, names, syntax, and immediate readability, rather than broader architectural goals. For instance, RMs for MM and MC saw substantial misalignment, with LLMs overlooking structural intentions behind these changes. In contrast, Pull Up operations had a near-perfect alignment, likely due to their localized semantics. Human raters, instead, often based their evaluations on project-wide consistency, long-term maintainability, and design abstraction, factors that are invisible in the local code snapshot available to the LLM. This gap reveals that while LLMs can mimic reasoning for simple refactorings, they fall short in capturing RMs rooted in architecture or foresight. 1. Local vs Structural Reasoning: LLM-generated RMs should be interpreted as partial approximations. They are effective for routine, localized changes but unreliable for strategic or architectural reasoning. To close this gap, future tools could expand LLM context with project-wide metadata or history-aware embeddings. According to RQ 2 , only 53% of LLM-generated RMs aligned exactly with the prior reference study. However, in 22% of the cases, LLMs enriched the rationale by adding context-specific nuances or detailing effects on testability, naming conventions, or structural clarity. These elaborations were never contradictory; instead, they made tacit developer knowledge explicit. This ability to extend RMs aligns with the finding that LLMs consistently emphasized clarity, maintainability, and readability. For example, when humans described motivation as "renaming, " the LLM often contextualized it in terms of onboarding ease or cognitive load, surfacing deeper reasoning that might otherwise be lost. Our study investigated the motivations behind performing code refactoring by employing LLMs on the version-control history data associated with the refactoring, compared their output to human rationale, as well as to the referenced prior study [65] . Moreover, we studied the extent to which product and process metrics can describe such RMs by analyzing their feature importance and correlation levels. Our results reveal that while LLMs agree with human judgment in most cases, they often diverge in deeper, architectural reasoning, favouring local, surface-level cues over systemic design intent. Still, LLMs demonstrate value in extending and clarifying RMs, surfacing implicit knowledge that is often under-documented. We further showed that most LLM-derived RMs are pragmatic, driven by clarity and simplification, rather than architectural ideals. SMs to depict developer experience and code readability proved informative but insufficient as standalone signals, reinforcing the need for hybrid solutions. Future research should focus on developing context-aware, LLM-guided refactoring recommendation systems that integrate both behavioural signals, such as RMs, and project-level insights. Similarly, future work should exploit the potential of further exploring prompting techniques, e.g., using multi-turn prompts, system-level metadata, or dependency graphs as prompt context. We believe such studies would provide LLMs with a more holistic analysis of the context involving the refactoring operation. LLMs can enhance traceability, documentation, and onboarding when paired with system context and developer interaction data. For researchers, this opens a space to explore enriched prompting, system-aware modeling, and empirical evaluation of hybrid systems. For practitioners, LLMs offer an opportunity to make the "why" behind code changes visible, fostering better collaboration and maintainability. LLMs do not just replicate developer intent; they can help understand, explain, and extend it. The next challenge is building tools that channel this capability with precision, context, and reliability. items.venue: Journal of Economics, Finance And Management Studies
items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

The unit of analysis was the individual organizational member even though the core constructs were judged through respondents’ informed views of their SMEs. Eligible participants comprised SME owners, senior and middle managers, finance and accounting professionals, financial analysts, data analysts, information technology specialists, and staff engaged in AI-supported financial, analytical, or managerial work. Respondents needed to work in SMEs based in emerging markets and to understand how their firms applied financial forecasting, business analytics, or AI tools in decision processes. This profile mattered because the paper frames strategic financial decision quality around choices on investment, liquidity, financing, and resource allocation under uncertainty. Generative AI-enabled financial forecasting capability captured the organizational ability to apply generative AI for integrating and interpreting financial information, producing forward looking financial diagnostics and predictions, and converting those outputs into useful input for financial planning and decisions, following the conceptualization drawn from Metzger et al. (2025) and related forecasting work. Business analytics capability measured the firm’s capacity to combine technological, human, data, and managerial resources and turn organizational data into analytical insights that support managerial action (Ashrafi et al., 2019; Awan et al., 2021). AI governance maturity reflected the degree to which formalized governance rules, responsibilities, processes, oversight arrangements, and technological mechanisms were applied consistently to keep AI use aligned with organizational, ethical, and legal requirements (Mäntymäki et al., 2022; Papagiannidis et al., 2025). Before the main survey the questionnaire was reviewed by academic experts and practitioners familiar with SME financial management, AI, business analytics, and organizational governance to check wording clarity, construct relevance, and content validity. A pilot study with eligible respondents then identified ambiguous wording and allowed minor refinement ahead of full data collection. The final questionnaire was distributed electronically through professional networks, SME associations, business contacts, and relevant online channels. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and respondents learned of the academic purpose of the study and the confidentiality of their answers. After screening for incomplete responses, duplicates, patterned answers, and low engagement, 385 valid questionnaires remained for statistical analysis. Initial screening checked missing values, response patterns, possible outliers, and overall suitability of the data for multivariate work. Internal consistency reliability was evaluated with Cronbach’s alpha. This step wa s especially useful because the conceptual framework separates forecasting capability from the broader organizational capacity to convert data into analytical knowledge. These results suggest that SMEs make better strategic financial decisions when they can generate for ward looking financial insights through generative AI and combine organizational data with effective analytical capabili ties. Generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability shows the larger standardized coefficient, highlighting the value of timely finan cial forecasts and prospective insights when managers assess risks, compare alternatives, and make financing, inve stment, liquidity, and resource allocation decisions. Business analytics capability also plays an important role by helping firms organize, inte rpret, and turn available data into evidence that can inform financial judgment. At the same time, AI governance maturity significantly strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality. This moderating effect is reflected in the positive interaction coefficient of B = 0.518 and the c onfidence interval from 0.437 to 0.599, which does not include zero. The result indicates that AI generated financial forecasts become more useful for strateg ic decisions when SMEs have clearer responsibilities, appropriate oversight, validation procedures , monitoring mechanisms, and risk Overall, the empirical results support H1, H2, and H3 and are consistent with the proposed framework linking generative AI en abled financial forecasting capability, business analytics capability, AI governance maturity, and strategic financial decision qua lity. Regarding the first research question, the findings establish that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability has a significant positive influence on strategic financial decision quality. The second research question is addressed by showi ng that business analytics capability also contributes positively to strategic financial decision quality, although its standardized coefficient is lower than that of generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability. For the third research question, the findings demonstrate that higher AI governance maturity strengthens the positive relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality. Taken together, the results suggest that emerging mar ket SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting capability is accompanied by broader analytical competence and sound governance arrangements. Improving strategic financial decision quality therefore involves not simply adopting advanced AI tools, but developing the organizational ability to interpret financial information, apply analytical insights, maintain appropriate human oversight, validate AI generated outputs, and establish clear responsibility for AI supported financial decisions. The empirical findings strongly support H1, as generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability significantly improves strategic financial decision quality with β = 0.613. This result strongly concurs with Metzger et al. (2025), who argue that genera tive AI can provide SMEs with accessible and timely financial diagnostics, and with Cheng et al. (2026), whose evidence demonstrates the predictive value of ChatGPT generated financial factors. It also reinforces Pelster & Val (2024), who associate ChatGPT based financial assessments with subsequent earnings and stock returns. However, the findings do not support an unqualified technological determinism in which stronger predictive capability automatically guarantees better decisions. Wasserbacher & Spindler (2022) caution that prediction cannot establish the causal knowledge required for planning, while Metzger et al. (2025) emphasize organizational readiness and managers’ ability to interpret AI outputs. The sizeable coefficient therefore suggests that forecasting capability matters, but not that managerial judgment becomes redundant. The findings strongly support H2, demonstrating that business analytics capability positively affects strategic financial dec ision quality with β = 0.487. This result strongly concurs with Awan et al. (2021), who associate big data analytics capability wit h higher decision-making quality, and supports Ashrafi et al. (2019), who contend that analytics capability creates organizational value through improved information quality and agility. Nevertheless, the comparatively lower coefficient than that of genera tive AI enabled financial forecasting capability challenges any assumption that broader analytics capability necessarily constitutes the dominant driver of strategic financial judgment. More importantly, the findings only partially support a technology cen tered interpretation of analytics. Mamakou (2026) argues that analytics value emerges from complementary technical, human, and contextual capabilities, while Awan et al. (2021) emphasize data driven insights as a mechanism connecting analytical resourc es with decision processes. The evidence therefore favors analytics as an organizational capability rather than a technological a sset operating independently. analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. First, the cross-sectional design captures organizational perceptions at one point in time and therefore cannot establish how generative AI forecasting, analytics capability, governance maturity, and financial decision quality evolve together. Second, the reliance on self-reported assessments may introduce common method and perceptual bias, particularly because organizational capabilities and decision quality were evaluated by individual respondents. Third, purposive sampling improves access to knowledgeable participants but restricts statistical generalization to the broader population of emerging market SMEs. Although the study covers heterogeneous organizational contexts, institutional, technological, and financial conditions can differ substantially across emerging markets. Finally, strategic financial decision quality is perceptual rather than based on objective decision outcomes. The results should therefore be interpreted as evidence of theoretically specified associations rather than definitive causal effects. Future research should extend the framework longitudinally to determine whether improvements in generative AI forecasting capability precede sustained improvements in strategic financial decision quality. Multi respondent designs could combine assessments from owners, financial managers, and technology specialists to reduce single informant dependence. Researchers could also complement perceptual decision quality with objective indicators such as forecasting errors, financing costs, liqu idity outcomes, or investment performance. Cross country studies would be particularly valuable for examining whether institutional development, regulatory environments, digital infrastructure, or financial market conditions alter the relationships identifi ed here. Further work should also investigate whether AI governance has nonlinear effects, since increasingly formal governance may not generate proportionately greater decision benefits. Finally, extending the model to human AI collaboration, managerial financ ial literacy, data quality, and organizational readiness could clarify the mechanisms through which AI generated forecasts become strategically useful financial knowledge.

items.title: What is Hybrid Intelligence? Toward a Multi-Layered Model for Complex Problem-Solving
items.venue: International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin, Predictive Maintenance, Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), Industry 4.0, Fault Detection, Condition Monitoring, Remaining Useful Life (RUL).

items.venue: Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic. Social implications In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs. Originality/value The study extends entrepreneurship education ecosystem thinking by treating AI as an active mediator of cognition and venture artifact production whose educational role depends on tool function, assessment design and institutional governance.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

items.title: From policy to pedagogy: a thinking-centered framework for epistemic agency in AI-enabled higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has challenged longstanding assumptions about the relationship between academic performance and student learning. When AI can generate essays, analyses, explanations and solutions, final products may no longer provide sufficient evidence that students engaged in the reasoning processes those products are intended to represent. This conceptual and theoretical paper proposes the IDEA framework as a thinking-centered approach to AI-enabled pedagogy. Drawing on scholarship in learning theory, reasoning, assessment and generative AI, the framework distinguishes among critical, systematic and creative thinking and connects these capacities to deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning. It further incorporates epistemic offloading and epistemic agency to examine how cognitive responsibility is distributed between learners and AI. The framework considers assignment structure, disciplinary context and learner development to determine when AI should be restricted, guided, or integrated. It also emphasizes making student reasoning, judgment, reflection and intellectual ownership visible. By shifting the focus from regulating AI use to identifying the cognitive and epistemic work that must remain meaningfully with the learner, IDEA provides a concept-to-application model for aligning generative AI with the purposes of teaching, assessment and curriculum in higher education.

items.title: Securing the Foundation of AI: A Deep Dive into Dependency Management and Security in Deep Learning Frameworks

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Deep learning (DL) frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch have powered major AI advancements, yet their reliance on third-party libraries introduces critical, understudied security risks. This article examines dependency management in these frameworks, focusing on dependency characteristics, associated vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies. We analyze 448 libraries, 8,641 dependency-related commits, and 72 vulnerabilities, using GitHub APIs, official package sites, NVD/CWE databases, and a developer survey. Our findings show that while both frameworks share similar dependency types, PyTorch has more dependencies with less frequent updates. Both exhibit substantial vulnerabilities—42 in TensorFlow and 30 in PyTorch—almost half of which are high or critical severity, many unresolved. Notably, cumulative vulnerability exposure events reach 9,653 for TensorFlow and 627 for PyTorch, largely due to repeated removal and reintroduction of vulnerable dependencies. We also reveal that most security fixes occur incidentally alongside dependency optimization or compatibility improvements. Only 12% of changes explicitly address security, despite 90% of developers acknowledging its importance, reflecting limited experience, over-reliance on dependencies, and unclear accountability. This study sheds light on dependency management practices in DL frameworks, highlighting critical security risks and offering actionable guidance to strengthen DL ecosystem security and resilience.

items.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

analysis.discussion: Generative AI can amplify or erode cognitive capital, and short-term outputs do not reveal which is happening. Four concepts emerge from this review. First, cognitive capital is a renewable and depletable stock of knowledge, capabilities and practices that people and organizations can mobilize; it is distinct from the capability of the human-AI system, so joint performance can improve while human capacities weaken. Second, assisted performance is not retained competence: growth in cognitive capital requires evidence of retention, transfer or improved collective capacity, not better output alone. Third, the effects of AI depend jointly on technology, design and use; the same models can substitute for practice or scaffold it, and can either calibrate or inflate trust. Fourth, individual gains do not automatically become organizational cognitive capital, which depends on how knowledge is codified, shared and kept diverse. Taken together, these concepts reframe the question organizations usually ask about AI. The relevant question is not only whether a tool improves productivity, but which human capacities it exercises, which it replaces and which it leaves unpracticed. This reframing connects three literatures that are rarely read together: learning science, which separates performance from learning [18] ; organizational research, which treats absorptive capacity and routines as collective assets [20] ; and extended-mind theory, which treats tools as potential components of cognition [5] . Cognitive capital offers a common unit for these perspectives because it asks what remains available to people and organizations when systems change, fail or are replaced. It also makes visible a tension in the evidence: the more capable and fluent an assistant becomes, the easier it is to accept its outputs without the effort through which competence is built and judgment is calibrated. Managing this tension requires deliberate choices about when AI should support, challenge or step back. This tension will become more pressing as AI systems move from answering requests to executing multistep tasks with less human involvement. As agents take on more of the work, the gap between what a human-AI system can do and what people can still do without it may widen, and the capacities needed to supervise, correct or replace those systems may be among the first to erode. Treating cognitive capital as an organizational asset to be measured, renewed and protected, alongside financial and human capital, is one way to keep that gap visible and governable. These concepts are organized into four mechanisms, seven principles and testable propositions that remain hypotheses rather than a validated theory. Their value lies in turning a broad concern about AI and human capability into measurable questions that organizations and researchers can address together.

items.title: Generative AI feedback use and English writing self-regulation among Chinese non-English majors: a two-wave study of feedback literacy and writing anxiety

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction Generative AI chatbots now give students instant commentary on their writing, yet little is known about how engaging with that commentary relates to the self-regulatory capacities on which writing development depends. This study examined a chain mediation model in which generative AI feedback use is associated with writing self-regulation through feedback literacy and, in turn, second language writing anxiety. Methods Non-English-major undergraduates at three universities in Henan Province, China, completed two surveys 12 weeks apart in the 2026 spring semester (wave 1 N = 650; 520 retained, 80.0%). Wave 1 assessed generative AI feedback use and feedback literacy; wave 2 assessed writing anxiety and writing self-regulation. Serial mediation analysis used 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples, with item-level validity checks and re-estimations without item parcels added as sensitivity analyses. Results Generative AI feedback use was positively associated with later writing self-regulation [ c = 0.265, 95% CI (0.190, 0.339)]. The total indirect effect was 0.128 [0.094, 0.167], or 48.3% of the total association: 0.086 [0.053, 0.122] via feedback literacy, 0.024 [0.008, 0.049] via writing anxiety, and 0.018 [0.009, 0.031] for the serial route. The direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137). Focal paths kept their signs and significance when item parcels were removed and when only feedback-seeking items defined the predictor. Discussion These estimates describe associations rather than effects of an intervention. With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. The pattern is consistent with a theoretically proposed ordering; the pedagogical suggestions are recommendations only, not demonstrated outcomes. The generative AI feedback use scale is a preliminary study-specific measure.

reading.interpretation: The question motivating this two-wave study was how generative AI feedback use relates to writing self-regulation among Chinese non-English-major undergraduates, with feedback literacy and writing anxiety positioned as sequential linking processes. Every hypothesis received support. Wave-1 generative AI feedback use was positively associated with wave-2 writing self-regulation ( c = 0.265), and about half of that association (48.3%) was represented by the two estimated indirect routes. The route through feedback literacy alone dominated (specific indirect effect = 0.086); smaller routes ran through writing anxiety alone (0.024) and through the serial chain from feedback literacy to writing anxiety (0.018), and the direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137), a partial-mediation pattern. Three framing points bound the interpretation. First, the estimates are unstandardized and drawn from a non-experimental design, so they describe covariation among naturally occurring variables rather than effects of an intervention. Second, separating the predictor and first mediator (wave 1) from the second mediator and outcome (wave 2) strengthens the temporal reading of the chain relative to single-occasion designs ( Maxwell and Cole, 2007 ), though without conferring causal status. Third, the participants were non-English majors, the population whose feedback access has historically been most constrained; English majors, whose curriculum supplies denser feedback environments, may show different patterns. Within these bounds, the consistency of the pattern across estimation, bootstrap, and sensitivity checks gives the substantive reading a stable empirical base. Generative AI feedback use at wave 1 positively predicted feedback literacy (a 1 = 0.405, SE = 0.038, p < 0.001). At wave 2, feedback literacy negatively predicted writing anxiety (d 21 = −0.193, SE = 0.037, p < 0.001), while generative AI feedback use kept a smaller negative association with writing anxiety (a 2 = −0.104, SE = 0.036, p = 0.004). In the outcome equation, writing anxiety negatively predicted writing self-regulation (b 2 = −0.231, SE = 0.046, p < 0.001), feedback literacy predicted it positively (b 1 = 0.212, SE = 0.040, p < 0.001), and generative AI feedback use kept a significant direct association (c′ = 0.137, SE = 0.038, p < 0.001). The total association equaled 0.265 [SE = 0.036, p < 0.001, 95% CI (0.194, 0.337)]. Of the covariates, only year of study showed a small positive association with writing anxiety ( b = 0.064, p = 0.033); gender was unrelated to all three endogenous variables. analysis.discussion: The question motivating this two-wave study was how generative AI feedback use relates to writing self-regulation among Chinese non-English-major undergraduates, with feedback literacy and writing anxiety positioned as sequential linking processes. Every hypothesis received support. Wave-1 generative AI feedback use was positively associated with wave-2 writing self-regulation ( c = 0.265), and about half of that association (48.3%) was represented by the two estimated indirect routes. The route through feedback literacy alone dominated (specific indirect effect = 0.086); smaller routes ran through writing anxiety alone (0.024) and through the serial chain from feedback literacy to writing anxiety (0.018), and the direct association remained significant (c′ = 0.137), a partial-mediation pattern. Three framing points bound the interpretation. First, the estimates are unstandardized and drawn from a non-experimental design, so they describe covariation among naturally occurring variables rather than effects of an intervention. Second, separating the predictor and first mediator (wave 1) from the second mediator and outcome (wave 2) strengthens the temporal reading of the chain relative to single-occasion designs ( Maxwell and Cole, 2007 ), though without conferring causal status. Third, the participants were non-English majors, the population whose feedback access has historically been most constrained; English majors, whose curriculum supplies denser feedback environments, may show different patterns. Within these bounds, the consistency of the pattern across estimation, bootstrap, and sensitivity checks gives the substantive reading a stable empirical base. Three kinds of claim are kept separate below: associations the data support, a theoretically proposed ordering that a two-wave design cannot confirm, and pedagogical recommendations that go beyond the estimates. The first is reported in the Results; the second and third are explicitly labeled wherever they appear. This first-stage association was sizable: students who reported more active engagement with AI feedback on their English writing also reported higher feedback literacy (a 1 = 0.405). This is consistent with a theoretical account in which feedback literacy develops through feedback episodes, an account the present design does not test ( Chong, 2021 ; Molloy et al., 2020 ). Chatbots lower the cost of feedback-seeking to almost nothing: a student can obtain commentary on a draft at any hour without waiting for a teacher's availability or exposing a weak text to classmates ( Barrot, 2023 ; Warschauer et al., 2023 ). Students who take up this affordance accumulate far more feedback encounters than classroom conditions alone allow, and each encounter is an occasion for the micro-judgments that constitute feedback literacy: Is this comment about content or form? Is it correct? What should I change? Evidence that students' engagement with ChatGPT feedback travels together with their feedback literacy ( Zhan and Yan, 2026 ) fits this reading, and the present findings extend it forward in time: higher wave-1 use went with higher wave-1 feedback literacy, which in turn tracked the wave-2 outcomes. Among the indirect routes, the one through feedback literacy alone was the largest (0.086, roughly two-thirds of the total indirect effect of 0.128). In substantive terms, the association between AI feedback use and later writing self-regulation is statistically decomposed mainly through the feedback-literacy route rather than through affect or through familiarity with the tool. This placement of feedback literacy as the proximal conduit parallels the broader feedback literature, where what students do with feedback matters more than its delivery ( Hattie and Timperley, 2007 ; Winstone et al., 2017 ). It also tempers the over-reliance narrative. Concerns that AI commentary substitutes for student judgment ( Zhai et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2024 ) describe a real risk, but in this sample the use pattern that was measured, namely active seeking, checking, and integrating of AI suggestions, was associated with a competence that supports self-regulated writing rather than with its absence. Two qualifications sharpen this interpretation. The scale measured active engagement rather than sheer volume of use; students who paste a draft and accept the first output without reading it would not score high. The distinction matters because survey evidence links heavy, passive consumption of AI-generated content to weaker critical engagement ( Zou et al., 2024 ), whereas deliberate engagement suggests the opposite. In addition, feedback literacy and generative AI feedback use were measured in the same wave, so their association partly reflects shared method and moment; the longitudinal part of the chain begins at the transition to wave 2. Neither qualification undoes the route. An alternative reading of the first stage deserves attention. Both variables were self-reported at wave 1, so students who are generally enthusiastic and reflective might report more of everything. Three considerations weaken this reading. Both the outcome and the second mediator were measured 12 weeks later, so any response-style contribution would have had to survive the interval. The item-level measurement model separated the constructs empirically, with discriminant validity supported by the Fornell-Larcker comparisons and heterotrait-monotrait ratios reported above. And the covariates, though limited to gender and year of study, captured no compositional route through which such a style would operate. Still, a dispositional common cause cannot be excluded with two-wave data, and future work should include baseline measures of the mediators and the outcome to address it directly ( Hamaker et al., 2015 ; Maxwell and Cole, 2007 ). The second stage of the chain connected competence to emotion. Students with higher feedback literacy at wave 1 reported lower writing anxiety at wave 2 (d 21 = −0.193), and lower anxiety in turn accompanied stronger writing self-regulation (b 2 = −0.231). Control-value theory provides a coherent reading of both links, and its application here extends the theory's control sources to a feedback-competence domain. Anxiety arises when an outcome is valued but control over it is doubtful ( Pekrun, 2006 ); feedback literacy is precisely a set of capacities that raise felt control over the feedback-and-revision cycle, from judging comments to converting them into concrete revisions ( Carless and Boud, 2018 ; Molloy et al., 2020 ). items.title: Generative AI and Cognitive Autonomy in Cameroonian Higher Education: A Conditional Amplification Framework for Learning

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.

reading.interpretation: This study examined not whether generative AI is intrinsically beneficial or harmful, but under what conditions its pedagogical use is associated with cognitive autonomy and deep learning. Across six Cameroonian higher-education institutions, GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation; self-regulation and cognitive engagement formed a significant sequential indirect pathway to ACA; ACA was strongly associated with deep learning; and AI literacy and institutional governance showed positive but modest moderation effects. The interview evidence qualified these average relationships by revealing both reflective, dialogic use and cognitive delegation. Generative AI does not remove the need for learner autonomy; it changes what autonomy requires. In this study, productive GAI use was associated with self-regulation, cognitive engagement and deep learning when users retained control over verification, strategy and intellectual responsibility. Interviews simultaneously showed that the same tools can encourage delegation and reduced effort. The central educational issue is therefore not simply access or frequency of use, but the quality of human-AI orchestration. The emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework offers a way to study that quality without treating technology and autonomy as opposites. For higher education in resource-diverse settings such as Cameroon, the implication is practical: expanding access to generative AI should be accompanied by AI literacy, pedagogical redesign and institutional guidance that protect human judgement. If these capabilities are unevenly distributed, GAI may amplify not only learning but inequality. items.title: Beyond access: the evolution of Portugal’s pharmacy-based vaccination strategy and the future role of AI-driven outreach

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

reading.overview: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example.
reading.interpretation: Portugal’s seasonal vaccination programme illustrates the value of combining community pharmacies and SNS services within a broad delivery network. Changes in the distribution of doses between settings do not, by themselves, demonstrate disengagement or identify the causes of remaining under-vaccination, and they do not suggest that the pharmacy model failed: it expanded the density of vaccination points and was strongly supported by the public ( 7 ). An independently conducted repetition of the survey on public satisfaction with pharmacy involvement in seasonal vaccination would help determine whether this initially high level of support has been sustained across subsequent campaigns. The next policy question is how to improve coverage through this combined infrastructure, building on existing invitations and recall while determining the relative contribution of confidence, motivation, and practical and residual access barriers, and testing interventions accordingly. Conversational systems, including generative AI, merit comparative evaluation as possible additions to these approaches. Their value should be established through incremental vaccination uptake, safety, equity, trust and cost-effectiveness, rather than assumed from technological capability. These conclusions rest on ecological, aggregate data that cannot establish individual-level causality, and the mechanisms discussed will require confirmation through prospective, patient-level research. Such evaluation should be conducted independently of any specific commercial provider, using transparent and predefined criteria.

items.title: Longitudinal association between AI dependence and pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition: the role of AI self-efficacy and perceived stress

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

items.title: Fact-Checking: A Survey on Content Verification in the Age of AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

items.title: Generative AI adoption and governance in universities: impacts on perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success in Southeast Asia

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: The International Journal of Information and Learning Technology
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

items.title: Weather warnings for a multilingual nation: The role of applied linguistics in the National Weather Service’s AI Language Translation Program

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

items.title: Workplace learning and AI challenges: causes and effects

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in workplaces is rapidly increasing in our society. This means that AI is fundamentally reshaping workplaces, how tasks are performed and how the authors interact with colleagues. This study aims to develop explanatory knowledge about the challenges of AI-augmented workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative and deductive research approach was applied. Key challenges discovered in the literature review were used as predefined themes to identify and analyse empirical data. Findings The authors have identified five key challenges: AI Strategy, AI Education, Control, Meaningfulness and Integrated Work Processes for Human-AI Collaboration. These challenges were examined in terms of their causes and effects, and an explanatory model (AICH) was developed. Research limitations/implications The study collected data from five companies, which provides some generality beyond this study’s empirical domain. However, it poses challenges in making broader generalisations. Future research could be designed as broader studies to confirm, modify or challenge the findings. Practical implications The findings contribute to workplace learning and provide a basis for identifying risks and potential measures. items.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

items.title: Beyond conversation length: Conversation openings, cognitive engagement, and support orientations in student-AI chatbot interactions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

items.title: Retrospective testing and prospective randomized trial of guardrails and a verifier for AI care plans

items.abstract_text: Abstract Health systems are adding verifiers, AI models that check another AI’s drafted care plans, to reduce errors and omissions. We tested a verifier in two ways. First, three AI models drafted care plans for 447 retrospective test cases; a verifier caught 5 of 17 errors checkable against the patient’s record when counting flags for wrong recommendations, and 10 of 17 when also including flags for missing care. Second, in a prospective trial (NCT07718893), we randomized 240 patients in complex primary care management programs in four states to unassisted physicians, physicians with a guardrailed AI assistant, or physicians with the guardrailed assistant plus a verifier. The verifier raised 11 alerts across 77 encounters; physician adjudicators judged 9 correct, but clinicians in the trial acted on only 1. Safety events were similar across arms. Effective verification may therefore require alerts that clinicians must resolve, despite the risk of alert fatigue.

The trial took place in Waymark’s multidisciplinary primary care service for Medicaid managed-care members in Ohio, Virginia, Washington, and Illinois. Waymark teams include community health workers, care coordinators, pharmacists, and therapists, supervised by physicians. Waymark enrolls members whom validated risk models identify as rising risk for emergency department visits and hospitalization33,34. Encounters came from the care team’s clinical rounds, which by default discuss patients with multimorbidity or polypharmacy; this enriched enrollment toward these patients, as pre- speciﬁed. Eligible patients wer e Medicaid-enrolled and attributed to a participating primary care site, with English-language documentation and an encounter that required clinical reasoning. We excluded patients with hospice- or palliative-care-exclusive care plans, patients enrolled in a competing AI-safety study within the prior 90 days, administrative-only or pharmacy-only encounters, and encounters in which the supervising clinician was the principal investigator. The sample size of 240 was ﬁx ed in the approved protocol. Speciﬁcity and aler t burden can be estimated when checkable errors are absent; sensitivity needs errors, so the trial could estimate it only if enough errors occurred. We randomized patients 1:1:1 with a deterministic HMAC-SHA256 permuted-block scheme (block size 6), stratiﬁed b y site. Allocation was concealed in the trial software. Physicians knew the arm from the drafting interface and were not blinded; outcome adjudicators were blinded. In Arm 1, the supervising physician wrote the assessment and plan without AI assistance. In Arm 2, Gemini 3.1 Pro drafted the assessment and plan under safety guardrails, and the physician reviewed, edited, and signed it. The guardrails had six parts (Supplementary Table 7): a safety system prompt that required a cited source and a conﬁdence le vel for every recommendation and prominent red ﬂags and safety hazards; retrieval of matching summaries from a curated library of society guidelines; a citation check that marked citations outside that library as unveriﬁed; four aut omated veriﬁcation checks (drug interactions, laboratory interpretation, guideline compliance, and a diagnostic safety net); a second- opinion consensus check; and a privacy ﬁlter that r eplaced patient identiﬁers. The model ran at temperature 0.2. These guardrails represent the safety layer that health systems commonly add on top of a language model. In Arm 3, Gemini 3.1 Pro drafted the plan under the same guardrails, and CITE then checked the draft as a further layer before physician review. We chose Gemini 3.1 Pro as the drafting model because it had the highest MedQA accuracy (97.4%) among frontier models in a comparison of general-purpose models and clinical AI tools35. In all arms the supervising physician signed the ﬁnal note CITE (version cite-1.0) sends the language-model draft and structured patient context (age, sex, problems, medications, laboratory values, and history) to a second language model (Claude Opus 4.8). CITE does not retrieve guideline text at run time; the model applies its own guideline knowledge and labels each ﬂag for missing care with the certainty of the evidence. Each ﬂag carries a quote fr om the draft, a one-line rationale, and a severity; ﬂags for missing car e take their severity from the certainty label, with high certainty set to 3, and other ﬂags ha ve severity 2. A ﬂag of se verity 3 sets the displayed status to ESCALATE. The displayed status depends on severity, whereas the pre-registered thresholds depend on ﬂag type. CI TE showed its status and ﬂags in r eal time in a side panel beside the draft, and the physician kept full decision authority.
