We did not ﬁnd a lar ger randomized comparison of this kind in live care; the closest prospective study was a single-arm study of 98 patients12. Guardrailed drafts were similar to unassisted physicians on safety events (4.9% vs 5.1%), escalation, and time to decision, and emergency visits and hospitalizations were numerically lower with guardrails. This is the local evidence that governance groups ask for4. The conﬁdence inter vals do not exclude differences of several points in either direction. Two explanations could account for the gap between valid ﬂags and signed notes. All 5 ﬂagged unsupported statements stayed in the signed notes, and 1 of 4 valid ﬂags for missing car e led to a change. One explanation is automation bias19,20. In a randomized trial of 44 physicians trained in AI literacy, wrong AI suggestions lowered diagnostic accuracy by 14.0 percentage points (95% CI − 18.9 to − 9.1)21. In the randomized substudy of NOHARM, physicians with AI help often left out useful AI recommendations1, and other randomized studies of AI decision support found similar gaps13,25. Another explanation, which the trial could not test, is that clinicians judged some ﬂagged items not t o need a change. Two designs could close this gap: a ﬂag that the clinician must r esolve before signing, and a ﬂag sent t o the care team member who acts on it, such as the pharmacist for a medication The lower error rate in live drafts held even in rising-risk patients with many conditions and medications. items.title: Designing transparency in AI influencer marketing: a consumer–agency architecture

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

items.title: Perceived impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical learning and decision-making among internal medicine residents in Ethiopia: a mixed- methods study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

For clarity, a single puzzle represents one complete Parsons problem task. Each puzzle contains all the foundational elements a student would need: a problem description, the correct lines of code (which would eventually be scrambled), the expected program output, and associated Comma Separated Values (CSV) data where applicable. These 315 puzzles served as the consistent baseline across all three stages of the study. By feeding the exact same 315 puzzles to the LLM in Stage 1 and Stage 3, we were able to conduct a direct comparison of the AI’s distractor-generation performance before and after refinement. This study used a GenAI-assisted methodology and did not involve human participants, student data, personal data, or identifiable information. Human involvement was limited to the authors evaluating the generated outputs. In accordance with the institutional requirements for human research, formal ethics approval was not Stage 1: Initial generation of distractors To address RQ1, a prompt containing the topic, context (e.g., Traffic Flow Analysis), question description, correct code, detailed distractor generation instructions, output constraints, and a predefined JSON output format for each puzzle was provided to Gemini-2.5-flash. A temperature of 0.7 was used to allow sufficient variation in the generated distractors while maintaining reasonable output consistency. The prompt incorporated zero-shot CoT prompting which required the AI model to specify its pedagogical reasoning behind each task before producing the final output. For each puzzle, the model was instructed to generate two logic - based distractors and two method-based distractors. A logic-based distractor changes the reasoning within a computational step while preserving the overall procedure. For example, the target procedure is mean error – specifically, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) – but a distractor used Mean Squared Error – a similar procedure but logically incorrect. In contrast, a method-based distractor replaces the computational method with a different one, such as instead of calculating sum, median is used. In total, 315 puzzles with four distractors each resulted in 1,260 initial distractors. The model was also prompted to generate a corresponding pedagogical rationale for each distractor, articulating the specific student misconception it intended to assess. Stage 2: Evaluation of generated distractors Stage 2 evaluated the functional plausibility of the generated distractors. First, each puzzle was verified whether it contained four semantically plausible distractors: two logic-based distractors and two method- based distractors. Second, distractors of the same type had to target the exact same line of correct code. For example, if the AI generated two logic distractors, both distractors should offer incorrect variations of the same correct line, instead of entirely different parts of the program. To evaluate each distractor, we replaced the corresponding correct line with one generated distractor, producing a modified version of the original program. Then, it was further assessed through two program-level checks: compilability and output divergence. The first examined whether the modified program could still be compiled in a Python environment without any errors. The second assessed output divergence by comparing the modified program’s output against the output of the correct solution. A distractor was considered output- divergent when the modified program produced a different result, indicating a notable change in the behaviour of the program, rather than a surface-level change. These checks ensure distractors were not superficially created but introduce a meaningful change in program behaviour that mirrors a genuine student error. items.title: Cross-Attention or Concatenation? A Multi-Seed Empirical Study of Code-Comment Fusion for Pull Request Outcome Prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Predicting whether a pull request (PR) will be merged, rejected, or left unre solved is a recurring problem in empirical software engineering, yet it remains unclear how much explicit fusion of code changes and reviewer comments adds over simpler designs, and conclusions drawn from a single training run can be misleading. We report a multi-seed comparison of encoder-based fusion strategies on a retrospective dataset of 33,955 PRs from 155 projects, three platforms, and 12 programming languages. A CodeBERT–RoBERTa hybrid with bidirectional cross-modal attention is compared with concatenation and late-fusion variants, four alternative code encoders (GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeReviewer), unimodal baselines, and two re-implemented prior systems, using five random seeds per model. The cross-attention hybrid reaches 88.11% mean accuracy (sample SD 0.39 percentage points, pp) and outperforms its code-only counterpart in every seed (+1.85 pp; Holm-adjusted paired p = 0.008). How-ever, the seven best models lie within a 0.42 pp band, and cross-attention exceeds concatenation by only 0.34 pp on average across five encoders (positive for four of five, not significant for any single encoder); at one seed (42) the ordering of the two reversed. Review comments alone are about as informative as code alone, and combining them adds roughly 1.6–1.9 pp. Project identity is strongly associated with the outcome (Cram´er’s V = 0.60), so the random split used here probably overstates generalisation. All analyses are retrospective, use features that become available only after review, and exclude LLM-based baselines.

reading.interpretation: Our results suggest three practical lessons for work on PR outcome prediction. First, the main gain comes from modelling both modalities: adding comments to code, or code to comments, is worth about 1.6-1.9 pp, whereas the choice among cross-attention, concatenation, and several code encoders matters by tenths of a point. Practitioners with limited compute can therefore start with concatenation of pooled encoder outputs, which is simpler than cross-attention and statistically indistinguishable from it in most of our configurations. Second, fusion comparisons need multiple seeds: for CodeBERT+RoBERTa, the per-seed gap between cross-attention and concatenation ranges from -0.06 pp to +1.83 pp around a pooled mean of +0.88 pp, so a single seed can report anything from a near tie to a two-point cross-attention win. One of our seeds (42) happens to favour concatenation by a hair, while four favour cross-attention; the pooled comparison itself does not reach significance after Holm correction. Third, evaluation design may matter more than architecture. Whether the observed ordering of models survives project-held-out or chronological evaluation is an open question that this paper cannot answer.

items.title: Responsible AI in Education Through an Islamic Ethical Framework: Integrating Human Agency, Cognitive Autonomy, and Academic Integrity
items.venue: Journal Of Islamic Education And Intellectual Discourse (JIED)

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study synthesizes research on Responsible AI in education to develop an Islamic ethical framework that supports human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Method: We conducted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) using PRISMA 2020 and analyzed 50 articles published between 2022 and 2026 from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, and Google Scholar. Findings: Research has shifted from technology acceptance toward ethics and governance, although it remains dominated by higher education and cross-sectional designs. Responsible AI principles include transparency, accountability, fairness, and human oversight. The Islamic perspective strengthens these principles through maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah and the values of amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, and tabayyun. The relationship between AI and human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity is conditional: reflective and verified use tends to support these dimensions, whereas dependence may undermine them. Novelty: This review's findings point to a shift from governance-centered responsibility to moral-epistemic responsibility, with three propositions: tabayyun as an obligation of epistemic verification, hifẓ al-‘aql as an educational orientation, and integrating AI governance with moral-educational development. Contribution: This study provides a conceptual foundation for responsible AI use in Islamic education by placing human oversight, information verification, independent thinking, and academic integrity at its core. Future Research: Future studies should test these propositions through longitudinal and experimental designs and develop instruments that integrate Islamic ethical values, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Tujuan: Kajian ini bertujuan mensintesis penelitian mengenai Responsible AI dalam pendidikan untuk merumuskan kerangka etika Islam yang mendukung agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik. Metode: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) berdasarkan PRISMA 2020 dengan menganalisis 50 artikel terbitan 2022–2026 dari Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, dan Google Scholar. Temuan: Penelitian bergeser dari penerimaan teknologi menuju etika dan tata kelola, meskipun masih didominasi oleh pendidikan tinggi dan desain cross-sectional. Prinsip Responsible AI meliputi transparansi, akuntabilitas, keadilan, dan pengawasan manusia. Perspektif Islam memperkuatnya melalui maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah serta nilai amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, dan tabayyun. Hubungan AI dengan agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik bersifat kondisional: penggunaan reflektif dan terverifikasi cenderung mendukung, sedangkan ketergantungan berisiko melemahkan. Kebaruan: Temuan kajian ini mengarah pada pergeseran dari governance-centered responsibility menuju moral-epistemic responsibility, dengan tiga proposisi: tabayyun sebagai kewajiban verifikasi epistemik, hifẓ al-‘aql sebagai orientasi pendidikan, serta integrasi tata kelola AI dan pembentukan moral-edukatif. Kontribusi: Memberikan dasar konseptual penggunaan AI yang bertanggung jawab dalam pendidikan Islam dengan menempatkan pengawasan manusia, verifikasi informasi, kemandirian berpikir, dan integritas akademik sebagai inti. Penelitian Selanjutnya: Menguji proposisi melalui desain longitudinal, eksperimental, dan pengembangan instrumen yang mengintegrasikan nilai etika Islam, agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik.

analysis.methods: This study employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines to identify, select, evaluate, and synthesize research on the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education (Page et al., 2021) . The literature search covered five databases: Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, and Google Scholar. It covered publications from January 2022 to July 2026. The search strategy comprised three keyword groups: the technology group, including artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, and large language model; the education group, including education, learning, teaching, higher education, and K-12; and the responsibility and ethics group, including Responsible AI, ethics, academic integrity, human agency, cognitive autonomy, Islamic values, Islamic education, maqāṣ id, amanah, adab, and tabayyun. The basic search string was as follows: ("artificial intelligence" OR "generative AI" OR "ChatGPT" OR "large language model" OR "LLM") AND (education OR learning OR teaching OR "higher education" OR "K-12") AND ("Responsible AI" OR ethics OR "academic integrity" OR "human agency" OR "cognitive autonomy" OR "Islamic values" OR "Islamic education" OR maqāṣ id OR amanah OR adab OR tabayyun). We then adapted the search string to reflect the syntax and search characteristics of each database. The search yielded 187 initial records. We limited searches to publications in Indonesian or English and to the period from January 2022 to July 2026. We verified full-text open access availability during the eligibility assessment stage. Articles were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) they addressed the use of AI or generative AI in education; (2) they had a substantive connection to one or more dimensions of Responsible AI, human agency, cognitive autonomy, academic integrity, and/or Islamic ethical values; (3) they were published in Indonesian or English; (4) they were published between January 2022 and July 2026; and (5) they were available as full-text open-access publications. Articles were excluded if they (1) addressed only the technical aspects or effectiveness of AI, without relevance to responsibility, human agency, academic integrity, or Islamic ethical values; (2) were unavailable as full-text open-access publications; (3) were published in languages other than Indonesian or English; (4) fell outside the specified publication period; or (5) were duplicates. The literature selection process followed the PRISMA 2020 stages of identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion (Page et al., 2021) . At the identification stage, we retrieved 187 records from the five databases. After removing 41 duplicate records, 146 records remained for screening. We screened these records by title and abstract and excluded 68 articles that did not meet the relevance criteria. Specifically, these articles did not address AI or generative AI in education, lacked a substantive connection to Responsible AI, human agency, cognitive autonomy, academic integrity, or Islamic ethical values, or did not align with the research focus. The remaining 78 articles underwent full-text eligibility assessment. Of these, 28 were excluded because they did not meet the inclusion criteria. The primary reasons for exclusion were the absence of full-text open access, publication in a language other than Indonesian or English, publication outside the period from January 2022 to July 2026, a focus solely on the technical aspects or effectiveness of AI, or the absence of a substantive connection to responsibility, human agency, academic integrity, and Islamic ethical values. Accordingly, 50 articles met all inclusion criteria and were selected as the units of analysis for this study, as shown in Figure 1 . Data from the selected articles were extracted according to publication and study characteristics; the types of AI or generative AI examined; the principles and dimensions of Responsible AI, human agency, cognitive autonomy, academic integrity, and Islamic ethical values; and the studies' main findings and limitations. The extracted data were then categorized according to conceptual and thematic similarities, compared across publications, and descriptively synthesized to address the four research questions. These categorization and synthesis processes identified patterns in the findings, relationships among themes, and research gaps warranting further investigation (Chong et al., 2022; Page et al., 2021) .

Accordingly, conceptual principles should not be treated as equivalent to measured and validated constructs. This suggests that research on Islamic ethics and AI is beginning to move toward empirical investigation, but has yet to establish a consistent measurement system. The relationship between AI use, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity is conditional, depending on purpose, degree of dependence, patterns of human-AI interaction, reflective capacity, information literacy, and oversight quality. Thus, AI use frequency cannot serve as the sole indicator of its educational benefits or risks. A relatively consistent relationship emerges between cognitive offloading and critical thinking. Gerlich (2025) found a negative relationship between AI use and critical thinking, with cognitive offloading serving as an important mechanism. Tian & Zhang (2025) showed that AI dependence is associated with lower levels of critical thinking, with cognitive fatigue serving as a mediator and information literacy as a factor influencing this relationship. Zhai et al. (2024) also showed that excessive dependence on AI dialogue systems can affect users' cognitive abilities. However, cognitive offloading does not always indicate cognitive failure. Hooper (2025) distinguishes between using AI as a cognitive aid and dependence that reduces user engagement. Meanwhile, Si et al. (2026) identified variations in AI use patterns, ranging from using AI as a thinking partner to patterns involving higher levels of dependence. These findings indicate that AI can support cognitive processes when users continue to evaluate and reflect. However, risks may arise when AI replaces reasoning processes that users should undertake. In the dimension of human agency, AI is associated with humans' ability to control, evaluate, and decide how to use technology. Alasgarova & Rzayev (2025) showed that AI integration can alter teacher-student relationships and challenge instructional authority, whereas AI literacy can help teachers maintain professional control. Ghamrawi et al. (2026) view agency as an outcome of reciprocal relationships between individuals and technology, while Chaaban et al. (2025) found variations in pre-service teachers' agency patterns, ranging from relatively independent AI use to patterns involving greater dependence. These findings indicate that AI does not inherently strengthen or weaken human agency; rather, its effects are associated with literacy, reflective capacity, purposes of use, and the educational environment. A similar pattern appears in academic integrity. Chen et al. (2024) reported increased plagiarism after using ChatGPT, whereas H. M. Nguyen & Goto (2024) showed that direct questioning can produce lower estimates of cheating than indirect measurement techniques. These findings indicate that results based on self-reports should be interpreted with caution. In contrast, Salam et al. (2026) found that purposeful use of ChatGPT may be associated with better academic integrity, whereas excessive dependence was associated with lower academic integrity. This position aligns with the self-regulated learning approach and the social-cognitive agency perspective, which view behavior, individual capacity, and the environment as mutually influencing elements (Chaaban et al., 2025; Mouta et al., 2025) . Overall, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity relate more to how AI is positioned within the educational process than to its mere presence or frequency of use. Purposeful, reflective use with verification helps users retain control over cognitive processes and academic decision-making, whereas dependence, uncritical acceptance of outputs, and weak oversight increase the risk of reduced autonomy and integrity. Therefore, AI literacy, information literacy, metacognitive skills, source verification, and assessment design are important components of responsible AI implementation. items.title: Projective Fiction in the Citiverse: AI-Generated Speculation and Curated Immersion as Instruments of Urban Imagination

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The Citiverse promises to merge physical and virtual urban space, yet citizens already inhabit a pervasive immersive medium: the dispersed, screen-bound attention of the smartphone. This paper introduces Projective Fiction, a design-theoretical and practice-based framework in which speculative imagery generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and curated mixed-reality staging act as instruments of urban imagination rather than previews of construction. Building on Cedric Price's emancipation of architecture from the imperative of realisation, it argues that the speculative image constitutes a distinct way of knowing the possible city. The framework is examined through a practice-based case study: Guerilla Domus, an installation and public performance in the Johanniskirche in Schwäbisch Gmünd (Germany), opened on 18 September 2026. Visitors were invited to surrender their smartphones at a coffin at the west portal, then encountered two backlit AI-generated allegories of the Johannisplatz, a mixed-reality Pietà staged over the real square via HoloLens, and a live transnational link to Molfetta (Italy). The paper's central contribution is the paradox of the second immersion: curated immersion in urban digital layers presupposes a deliberate exit from the first, dispersed immersion, an exit that must be designed as a threshold. Observations from the opening, where guests readily donated old devices but most kept the phone in use and re-mediated the event through it, inform four design principles for civic immersive technologies: threshold, shared view, anchoring in place, and declared fiction. Projective Fiction is positioned as a humanistic counter-model within the Citiverse that expands rather than colonises urban imagination.

items.abstract_text: This qualitative case study examined how ten secondary school ESL students in Malaysia used ChatGPT when revising their writing. The study did not focus on writing scores. Instead, it looked at students’ writing behaviours, the decisions they made when using ChatGPT, and the changes that appeared between their first and revised drafts. The students first wrote an essay on “Having a Balanced Diet” without using ChatGPT. After a short introduction to the tool, students revised the same essay with the help of ChatGPT. Data collection took place through writing samples from the students and semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis, while the comparison between the first and the second drafts was conducted using document analysis. From the findings, it is clear that the students made use of ChatGPT to go through grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and content of their essays. Many improvements had been made in the revised drafts. Most of the students managed to fix grammar errors and use more suitable vocabulary, along with presenting new ideas in their work. Nonetheless, there are some flaws in the second drafts such as incorrect expressions, informal language and some incorrect ideas. The interviews also showed that the students did not accept the suggestions directly. The students chose those suggestions which were clear to them, appropriate to the task and related to their original meaning. Overall, the study shows that ChatGPT may be used to support ESL writing revision but students still need teacher guidance and their own judgement to use it critically and responsibly.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED ACOUSTIC ANALYSIS OF LEGAL DISCOURSE PROSODY: OPPORTUNITIES AND LIMITATIONS

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The article examines the methodological potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted acoustic analysis for investigating prosody in legal discourse. Prosody is viewed as an essential component of spoken legal communication, shaping the expression of epistemic stance, interpersonal relations, discourse organisation, and persuasive strategies through variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, pausing, speech rate, and voice quality. The study addresses the limited attention paid to the acoustic dimension of legal discourse and evaluates the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI technologies into prosodic research. The object of the study is the prosodic organisation of spoken legal discourse; the subject is the methodological potential and limitations of AI-assisted acoustic analysis of legal speech. The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. The research is theoretical and methodological, drawing on studies in acoustic phonetics, computational paralinguistics, forensic phonetics, legal linguistics, and speech processing. Descriptive, comparative, and criticalevaluative methods are applied to assess AI-assisted acoustic analysis according to six methodological criteria: validity, reliability, scalability, interpretability, ecological validity, and legal and ethical admissibility. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and scalability of acoustic analysis by automating speech preprocessing, feature extraction, and computational modelling, enabling large-scale investigation of authentic legal speech. At the same time, important limitations remain, including reduced ecological validity, limited model transparency, algorithmic bias, risks of overinterpreting acoustic evidence, and legal and ethical concerns. The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

items.title: Does Generative AI Reduce Mental Effort at The Expense of Deep Thinking? An Experimental Investigation of Cognitive Load and Knowledge Retention
items.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
items.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ). Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. Research limitations/implications This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

items.title: INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEMS AND ETHICAL OVERSIGHT IN AI-DRIVEN ORGANISATIONS: REDEFINING THE THEORY OF CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

items.venue: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
items.abstract_text: This study examined how internal control systems and ethical oversight shape corporate governance effectiveness in AI-driven organisations, using listed deposit money banks in Nigeria as the focus. The increasing use of artificial intelligence in banking operations has introduced governance risks that traditional control systems may no longer fully address. Previous studies mostly considered internal controls, ethics, and governance as separate issues, with limited evidence on how they work together in emerging economies. The study therefore assessed the effects of Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Monitoring Activities on Tobin’s Q, and also examined the moderating role of Ethical Oversight. A correlational and panel data research design was adopted. Secondary data were sourced from the audited annual reports and accounts of 13 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria for the period 2015 to 2024. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, Hausman specification test, and random effects regression were used for the analysis. The findings showed that all the internal control variables had positive and significant effects on Tobin’s Q, while Information and Communication had the strongest influence. Ethical Oversight also showed a positive direct effect and significantly strengthened the relationship between internal control systems and firm value. The study concludes that effective internal controls, when supported by credible ethical governance, improve market performance and broaden the traditional view of corporate governance in technology-driven institutions. It therefore recommends that deposit money banks strengthen risk management systems, widen internal audits to cover AI systems, establish active ethics committees, invest in secure digital reporting platforms, and provide continuous governance training for directors and compliance officers.

items.title: Gender diversity as a strategic governance capability in the age of AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper aims to reframe board gender diversity as a strategic governance capability rather than a symbolic initiative or universal performance lever. It explains inconsistent diversity–performance findings and clarifies when diversity may strengthen oversight in algorithmically mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on structured evidence mapping and interdisciplinary research in corporate governance, leadership, efficiency economics, organizational demography and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, the paper develops a structured integrative conceptual synthesis focused on power, expertise–authority alignment and technological oversight. Findings Diversity effects are contingent rather than automatic. Board gender diversity is most likely to strengthen governance when three enabling conditions are present: representation thresholds that convert presence into voice, expertise aligned with authority and inclusive power structures that enable challenge. Under algorithmic complexity, these conditions may strengthen oversight of bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, vendor dependence and technocratic capture. Practical implications Boards and policymakers should move beyond numerical representation to structural influence. Diverse directors should occupy consequential committees, have relevant expertise and decision rights and be supported by practices that enable challenge. Boards should evaluate participation, committee assignments and technology-governance structures so diversity contributes to accountability, risk oversight and resilience rather than symbolic compliance. Social implications Representation-focused reforms are insufficient when formal inclusion does not produce influence. More substantively inclusive governance can strengthen accountability and stakeholder responsiveness in algorithmic organizational environments. Originality/value The paper moves beyond the business-case debate by integrating intersectionality, governance, efficiency and AI-governance perspectives into a mechanism-based framework showing how board diversity becomes a strategic governance capability under algorithmic complexity.

items.title: Content licensing strategy in AI–publisher coopetition: the role of asymmetric comparative advantages and citation intensity

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

items.title: When knowledge conversion pays off: knowledge utilization and ethical AI climate for Generation Z employees’ job performance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose While organizational knowledge conversion (OKC) is central to value creation, its translation into individual employee performance remains insufficiently understood, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled contexts where knowledge is abundant but must be appropriately adapted and ethically applied to generate meaningful outcomes. Against this backdrop, this study aims to empirically examine how OKC influences employee job performance (efficiency, effectiveness and quality) through customization knowledge utilization (CKU). Moreover, this study aims to investigate the moderating role of ethical AI climate (EAIC) among Gen Z employees working in AI-enabled hospitality workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave, time-lagged survey was conducted among 423 employees working in 3-, 4- and 5-star hotels in India. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS for measurement model, hierarchical regression and Hayes’ PROCESS macro to test mediation and moderated-mediation effects. Findings The results show that OKC significantly enhances employees’ job efficiency, effectiveness and quality. CKU partially mediates these relationships, indicating that knowledge should be adapted to task-specific contexts for greater performance outcomes. Furthermore, EAIC strengthens the indirect effects of OKC on performance via CKU, suggesting that ethical norms surrounding AI use enhance responsible and effective knowledge application. Originality/value This study extends the knowledge-based view and socialization, externalization, combination and internalization model by linking knowledge conversion to individual-level performance outcomes. It introduces CKU as a key mediating mechanism and positions EAIC as a critical boundary condition in AI-enabled work environments. By focusing on Gen Z employees, the study contributes to emerging knowledge management research on digital-native workforces in AI-enabled workplaces.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose This exploratory study examines how two conversation-based AI models, ChatGPT (USA) and DeepSeek (China), frame fundamental political concepts, “freedom, equality, democracy, social order” and the role of the state within political communication. It aims to compare the normative priorities and ideological assumptions in their responses and assess their possible relationship with the geopolitical contexts of their development. Design/methodology/approach The research used a structured comparative design and qualitative content analysis. The dataset comprises English responses to six core questions posed to GPT-4 and DeepSeek Chat in April 2024, followed by standardized follow-up questions for five items. Analysis focused on discursive framing, value priorities, and implicit assumptions. Findings Both models generally use similar democratic discourses when explaining freedom, equality, and democracy, but differ in value prioritization. ChatGPT foregrounds individual autonomy, personal rights, and democratic processes, whereas DeepSeek emphasizes collective welfare, social harmony, and the state's responsibility to maintain social order. Both refer to democracy, the rule of law, and human rights at a general level. These patterns are exploratory and not generalizable. Practical implications The study highlights the importance for policymakers, technology developers, and media professionals of understanding ideological asymmetries in AI-mediated political communication, and stresses transparency and critical awareness in conversational AI systems. Social implications The implicit normative assumptions of conversational AI can influence political information acquisition, democratic discourse, and cross-cultural understanding. Their spread in everyday information environments may shape how users interpret political concepts in unseen ways. Originality/value The study treats generative AI not merely as a technological tool but as systems situated in different geopolitical contexts that can participate in shaping social-political discourse. Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek offers an empirical framework for assessing ideological positioning and normative differences in conversational AI.

items.title: The Emotion Economy: Algorithmic amplification, cognitive fluency, and cultural schemas in Instapoetry

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Current research on AI-enabled manufacturing transformation largely focuses on the firm-level dimensions of R&D, production or marketing, with few studies examining how AI drives manufacturing transformation at the ecosystem level. This study addresses this gap by investigating the AI-enabled reshaping paths of manufacturing firm innovation ecosystems (MFIE) from a dynamic capability perspective. Design/methodology/approach This multi-case study adopts a dynamic capability perspective to conduct comparative analysis of four typical manufacturing firms, with data triangulated from in-depth interviews, corporate archives and industry reports, thereby identifying both common patterns and differentiated paths of AI-enabled MFIE reshaping. Findings The reshaping path comprises three components: differentiated reshaping pressures as the trigger, AI-enabled dynamic capability construction as the mediator and inter-ecosystem coopetitive replacement as the outcome. At different reshaping stages, focal firms build AI-enabled opportunity identification, solution diffusion and standard locking capabilities to resolve corresponding pressures. Four distinct paths are identified: technology efficiency enhancement, emerging market expansion, independent R&D technology breakthrough and ecosystem platform dominance. Different AI application strategy combinations lead to heterogeneous dynamic capability effects, influencing reshaping outcomes. Originality/value Departing from the single-ecosystem evolution perspective, this study conceptualizes MFIE reshaping as coopetitive replacement between old and new ecosystems and constructs a dynamic capability-based path framework and classification matrix. The study provides actionable guidance for managers to select and implement reshaping paths and offers implications for industrial policy formulation.

items.title: The Emotion Economy: Algorithmic amplification, cognitive fluency, and cultural schemas in Instapoetry

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

items.title: AI-Driven Reliable SFC Deployment: Challenges, Opportunities, and Perspectives

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are driving increasing volumes of reliability-sensitive Service Function Chain (SFC) requests from applications such as autonomous driving, smart manufacturing, and intelligent healthcare. These applications require not only feasible deployment but also continuous service availability under failures, disruptions, and uncertainty. Existing reliable SFC deployment studies have largely relied on rule-based approaches, which provide explicit formulations and interpretable decision rules but often struggle with dynamic, large-scale, and multi-objective requirements involving reliability, latency, cost, and security. AI-driven solutions therefore offer a promising direction for enabling adaptive and data-driven deployment decisions. This survey first clarifies the workflow of SFC deployment and the distinction between conventional and reliable SFC deployment. We then review rule-based reliable SFC deployment, analyzing its major design rationales, representative solution paradigms, and limitations. Building on this analysis, we examine AI-driven methodologies for reliable SFC deployment, with a particular focus on deep reinforcement learning approaches, which dominate the existing literature. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward adaptive, robust, and scalable reliable SFC deployment.

items.abstract_text: Navigation and manipulation are core capabilities in Embodied AI, but training agents to perform them directly in the real-world is costly, time-consuming, and unsafe. Therefore, sim-to-real transfer has emerged as a key approach, yet the sim-to-real gap persists. This survey examines how physics simulators address this gap by analyzing properties that have received limited attention in prior surveys. We also analyze their features for navigation and manipulation tasks, as well as their hardware requirements. Additionally, we offer a resource with benchmark datasets, metrics, simulation platforms, and methods to help researchers select suitable tools while accounting for hardware constraints.

items.title: Explainable AI for tail-risk forecasting in cryptocurrencies: evidence from green and energy-intensive assets for risk-aware investment decisions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

items.title: Effect of Teledermatologist Supervision in AI Skin Cancer Apps on Patients’ Trust and Adherence Intentions: Randomized Controlled Trial

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

To address the proportional odds assumption violation for risk assessment, 2 binary generalized linear mixed model sensitivity analyses were conducted with the same predictors and participant random intercepts. The first contrasted high adherence intentions vs moderate/neglect; the second contrasted neglect vs high/moderate adherence, reflecting the theoretically motivated distinction between engagement (high and moderate) and disengagement (neglect). Main effects replicated across both models: hybrid source increased odds of high adherence intentions (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.08-1.94; P =.01), and high-risk assessment strongly reduced odds of neglect (OR 9.40, 95% CI 6.04-14.63; P <.001). Critically, the risk × motivation interaction replicated in the neglect model (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.25-0.78; P =.005), confirming that concern-motivated participants were significantly less likely to neglect a high-risk assessment compared to curiosity-motivated participants—consistent with the CLMM finding that the boost in adherence intentions from high risk was larger for concern than curiosity. The interaction did not reach significance in the high adherence intentions model ( P =.11), indicating that the effect is specifically concentrated at the disengagement threshold rather than the high engagement threshold. These analyses confirm that the CLMM findings are robust to the proportional odds violation. The relatively narrow CIs indicate that these effects were estimated with good precision. The CLMM—with participant as a random intercept—showed that greater trust significantly increased odds of stronger adherence intentions. Advice source had no main ( P =.29) or interaction effect ( P =.17), indicating trust’s influence on adherence intentions was consistent across sources (see Multimedia Appendix 7 ). These results suggest that trust mediates advice source’s effect on adherence intentions, supporting hypothesis H3, contrasting with H1b where advice source affected adherence when trust was not accounted for. The indirect effect of advice source on adherence intentions via trust was estimated as the product of 2 paths: source → trust and trust → adherence intentions, assessed through a Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 draws. To obtain unbiased estimates, both CLMM for trust’s effect on adherence (path b) and LMM for source’s effect on trust (path a) were rerun without any interaction terms. The CLMM showed a statistically significant negative effect of trust on adherence intentions (estimate=–0.030, SE =0.002; P <.001), indicating that higher trust predicted better adherence. The LMM revealed a highly significant and negative effect of AI source compared to the reference hybrid source (estimate=–11.20, SE =0.41; P <.001), indicating lower trust under AI-only advice. Combining these path coefficients, the indirect effect was estimated as 0.34 with a 95% CI (0.29-0.39), excluding zero and indicating good precision as well as full mediation (H3). The relatively narrow CI indicates that this mediated effect was estimated with good precision. This positive indirect effect suggests that hybrid advice sources increase adherence intentions by enhancing trust. Figure 4 provides an overview of the results of the main hypothesis tests.
analysis.discussion: This randomized controlled, vignette experiment aimed to answer the question “How do advice source (AI alone or Hybrid) and user motivation (curiosity vs concern) shape patient trust and adherence intentions to the provided advice within the context of AI-supported teledermatology?” The 879 participating adults reported trusting risk assessments from a hybrid source (AI plus a teledermatologist) more than AI-only assessments and reported higher intentions to follow the advice. Mediation analysis showed that trust fully explained this effect, meaning that hybrid advice increased adherence intentions by increasing the participants’ trust. A high risk of a malignancy (rather than a low risk) further strengthened the intention to follow the advice, particularly among participants who use the app out of concern rather than out of curiosity. Notably, the sensitivity analysis revealed that the interaction between motivational context and risk assessment level was specific to the disengagement threshold: concern-motivated participants were significantly less likely to neglect a high-risk assessment compared to curiosity-motivated participants, while the 2 groups did not differ substantially in rates of high adherence intentions. This suggests that users motivated by curiosity are more likely to neglect when receiving high-risk assessments, compared to users who are already concerned. From a health behavior perspective, this is consistent with protection motivation theory [ 55 ], which posits that threat appraisal motivates protective behavior most strongly when perceived vulnerability is high and personally relevant. Curiosity-driven users—who may perceive themselves as less personally at risk—may be more prone to dismissing unexpected high-risk findings as a false alarm. The results also identified trust as the central mechanism through which hybrid advice improves adherence intentions, highlighting the value of integrating teledermatologist supervision into AI-driven skin cancer apps to maximize triaging efficiency. An overview of the main results can be found in Figure 4 . Our findings differ slightly from those of Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ], who found that the mediators between increased patient compliance and human physician supplementing AI were perceived social presence and innovativeness, suggesting multiple mediating factors are induced by human clinician presence. Similarly, Reis et al [ 57 ] found patients preferred human-only chat responses for reliability, empathy, and willingness to follow advice, compared with an AI chatbot or a hybrid chat. Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ] presented AI in a positive manner and communicated a clear purpose, mentioning AI’s capability in diagnosing skin lesion photos. In contrast, Reis et al [ 57 ] used chatbot transcripts without clarifying AI’s role, possibly explaining the preference for human-only advice rather than hybrid. These findings suggest hybrid advice works best when users understand the AI’s purpose, not as a full substitute for human care [ 58 ]. Therefore, it is recommended to ensure patients understand the purpose of AI’s involvement, alleviating patients’ concerns about losing human involvement in health care [ 59 ], and for making human-AI collaboration more effective. Although including a human teledermatologist was found to increase the likelihood of higher adherence intentions by a factor of 1.7, and users’ trust in the assessment from 66% to 77%, always including human teledermatologist supervision may be increasing workload too much [ 26 ]. Both AI-alone and hybrid models are more cost-effective postreferral than face-to-face assessments without AI [ 26 ], but only offering teledermatology to cases where the AI assessment is high risk, or shifting the usage of AI to postreferral by a primary health care provider, may be an effective compromise, depending on the intervention requirements and goals. This is particularly relevant given that Smak Gregoor et al [ 30 ] found that low-risk app assessments failed to prevent unnecessary appointments, tripling benign lesion claims. Offering teledermatology review to concerned users with low-risk assessments may be a strategy to prevent in-person appointments, depending on the health care system. To avoid users neglecting high-risk assessments, strategies are required to ensure that those who use the app out of curiosity take the assessment seriously. High-risk assessments may require tailored messaging for users who do not present with preexisting concern, to prevent disengagement in precisely the cases where action is most warranted. Our study provides insights on intended adherence to low-risk/benign assessments—reflecting most real-world cases—rather than comparing stage 0 skin cancer with stage 2 as did Soellner and Koenigstorfer [ 56 ], which represents the minority of cases. Thus, our results provide insights into drivers of patients’ adherence intentions prior to triaging, which is crucial for avoiding overdiagnosis [ 9 , 30 ]. It is worthy of noting that the vignettes in our study altered the motivation (curiosity vs concern), which is intertwined with perceived lesion risk. This was done intentionally to create credible vignettes. However, it is plausible that a user of an app has low perceived lesion risk and is not curious but is using the app for other reasons. Further research could investigate whether using the app because it was encouraged by a family doctor, or family member, or for any other reason influences adherence to the app’s advice. Our study did not consider costs of teledermatology integration, so AI-only solutions may be more cost-effective despite lower adherence intentions and trust although hybrid solutions appear to be most effective postreferral [ 26 ]. The study sample was drawn from the Erasmus MC Patient Panel, representing highly engaged health care users with typically higher digital literacy and education levels than in the general population, which may limit generalizability. The vignette-based experiment involved participants experiencing hypothetical scenarios, and stated trust and adherence intentions may not fully reflect behavior during actual app use. The use of predetermined simulated app outputs rather than participant-uploaded images prioritizes internal validity by isolating the effects of advice source and risk level, though it may reduce perceived personal relevance compared to a real app scenario. However, vignette responses have been shown to correspond closely with real clinical behavior [ 60 ], and relative comparisons between conditions are generally robust to hypothetical bias [ 61 , 62 ]. The mixed design—with motivational context as a between-participants factor and advice source and risk level as within-participants factors—allowed for controlled manipulation of key variables while accounting for individual differences. items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p &lt; 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. Originality/value The paper theorizes AI not as a tool within the firm but as a boundary-spanning coordination mechanism coupling sociotechnical and institutional domains. The dual-axis typology, tested attribution asymmetry and three propositions provide a foresight-driven framework for understanding strategic readiness in B2B transformation.

items.title: Learning-consequential assessment: making learning count when students use generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI can enable production without corresponding learning, yet wholesale exclusion from assessed work forgoes opportunities needed for workplace and lifelong learning. This article proposes learning-consequential assessment design. Students may use AI to produce assessed work, but success also depends on showing they possess the understanding their AI-supported work displays. Knowing this may encourage students to use AI for learning through explanation, comparison and challenge, rather than product optimisation alone. The central claim, that the understanding displayed is the learner's own, rests on coherence between their reasons for consequential decisions and their work, with independent performance corroborating where needed. Evidence may also warrant three capability claims: learner-directed production with AI, accountable verification of AI-shaped work and independent capability. Learning Orchestration describes the cognitive-metacognitive, epistemic and ethical judgement through which learners coordinate AI and other resources for learning, production and verification; teacher orchestration describes how teaching and assessment support its development.
