items.title: AI digital humans and destination marketing: the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism, parasocial interactions and marketing effectiveness

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) digital humans, developed to mimic humans, have emerged as promoters in marketing. Although existing studies have identified that AI digital humans' anthropomorphism shapes marketing outcomes, the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism remains underexplored. Focusing on historical figure-inspired AI digital humans in tourism destination marketing, this study examines how their multiple anthropomorphic features influence consumers' responses under the Computers are Social Actors and Media are Social Actors paradigms. Design/methodology/approach An online survey (N = 435) was conducted in 2026. Respondents completed a questionnaire after watching a typical travel vlog featuring a historical figure-based AI digital human. Findings We revealed that voice, behavior and mental anthropomorphism influence consumers' parasocial interactions with AI digital humans, which subsequently affect consumers' attitudes toward tourism destinations. Mental anthropomorphism mediates appearance, voice and behavior anthropomorphism's effects on parasocial interactions. Furthermore, mental anthropomorphism's effect is conditioned by consumers' familiarity with the AI digital human's historical figure prototype. Research limitations/implications This study extends existing research by demonstrating that AI digital humans' multiple anthropomorphic features shape consumers' parasocial interactions, with historical figure familiarity serving as a moderator. However, nonprobability sampling and a single cultural context restrict generalizability, warranting cross-cultural research with probability sampling in the future. Practical implications This study provides practical insight into developing AI digital humans in tourism marketing. Marketers should systematically optimize their human-likeness across voice, behavioral and mental traits, while considering consumers' individual differences. Originality/value This study fills the research gap in AI digital humans by unpacking the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism and showing that its effects are contingent on consumers' traits.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used within higher education to enhance curriculum design, automate academic tasks, and personalise learning. Despite this, little is known about teaching academics’ attitudes, intentions and behaviours and in turn, how they use and plan to use GenAI in practice. This qualitative study explored teaching academic staff attitudes, intentions and behaviours regarding their use and future use of GenAI. Data was collected via five open ended questions focusing on current teaching practices. The Theory of Planned Behaviour informed the analytical process. Academic staff were drawn from 20 different disciplines across 24 countries. Six main themes were identified: Efficiency and Automation, Ethics and Authenticity, Quality, Customised Learning, Institutional Policy-Practice and Sociocultural Implications. Overall, there was a dichotomy in responses. Participants noted that while GenAI could streamline teaching and enhance resource quality, it might also increase short-term workload and reduce the role of human judgement, risking unreliable outputs. They also highlighted limited institutional policies, strategies, and training. These attitudes have implications for updating policies, practical strategies, and meaningful training in higher education institutions.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval. The findings not only confirm their adaptability in enhancing existing systems but also open up exciting possibilities for their deployment in specialised web information domains, paving the way for future research in this evolving field.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare
items.abstract_text: Connected health integrates sensors, mobile devices, and information technology to realize the real-time collection and transmission of medical data, providing patients with more personalized and efficient medical services. In this context, medical image segmentation technology plays a vital role as a key digital medicine tool in connected health. However, its effective deployment across diverse clinical settings and data sources remains challenging due to inherent variations in imaging modalities, patient demographics, and device characteristics. Currently, connected health requires highly efficient AI models for real-world medical applications. The versatility of the model across diverse environments is of great significance. Domain Generalization (DG) has emerged as a crucial solution to address these challenges of connected health. Previous work focuses on the domain similarity calculation on the final layer output of the backbone model, which ignores the impact of the multi-scale features. In this article, we proposed a Domain Pyramid Attention Network (DPANet), which aims to transfer knowledge from source domains to unseen domains for medical image segmentation at a multi-scale level. The overarching goal is to enhance the efficiency of connected health systems through this innovative knowledge transfer mechanism. DPANet is capable of learning multi-scale similarity between two kinds of domains through a Domain Similarity Pyramid Attention Module (DSPAM). We also designed Domain Prototypes (DP), which can enhance the flexibility of the knowledge pre-extracted from source domains for better transferability. A simple fusion method is adopted to merge the multi-scale features for the final segmentation prediction. DPANet is evaluated on Brain Tumor segmentation and Retina Fundus segmentation tasks, achieving an average Dice improvement of 1.14% and 0.98% on these two tasks, respectively.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract AI-supported agricultural advice raises questions about useful information, the responsibilities of providers and the accessibility of legal-rights information. This study examines stated preferences about these issues in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh. The mixed sample consists of law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents; the workbook does not identify farmers, agricultural AI users or actual knowledge of farmers’ legal rights. The analysis therefore examines questionnaire responses about rights information and safeguards rather than claiming to measure farmers’ rights awareness or the effects of an AI service. Individual items are reported using descriptive distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory rank correlations with Holm adjustment. Of 385 respondents, 338 (87.8%) endorsed including legal-rights information in responsible digital agricultural services, 330 (85.7%) endorsed identifying responsibility for important advice, 325 (84.4%) endorsed communicating uncertainty and limitations, and 247 (64.2%) endorsed human assistance when AI advice is inadequate. The rights-information item exceeded the usefulness item by 24.4 percentage points; 215 respondents endorsed both. The statements differ in content, and their paired comparison does not identify the effects of a service or rank the value of its features. Exploratory correlations with the rights-information item were small and did not provide clear evidence of association after adjustment for four tests. The article distinguishes information about rights from demonstrated legal knowledge and recommends evaluation with identified agricultural users, specific legal scenarios and observable referral pathways.

items.title: AI Skin Analysis in Real-World Practice: A Multi-Source Evidence Assessment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized to support the early assessment of skin lesions. While numerous studies report high diagnostic accuracy under controlled experimental conditions, considerably fewer integrate technical validation, independent clinical stress-testing, and large-scale real-world evidence (RWE) within a single transparent framework. Objective: To evaluate the capabilities, clinical utility, and operational limitations of a mobile AI-assisted skin analysis system by synthesizing three complementary streams of evidence. Methods: This study integrates: (1) an analysis of longitudinal technical performance metrics and big-data usage patterns from over 6.57 million real-world smartphone assessments; (2) an independent clinical evaluation ((n = 160) analyzed cases) conducted at a specialized tertiary referral dermatology center comparing AI predictions and triage routing against histopathological, cytological, or expert clinical reference standards; and (3) a comparative synthesis with contemporary peer-reviewed literature, including external validation on skin of color. Results: Longitudinal technical validation demonstrated consistent, balanced improvements across sensitivity (97.4%), specificity (93.1%), and overall accuracy (94.2%) by 2026. In real-world consumer usage, common inflammatory conditions (e.g., acne/rosacea, (n = 708,356)) accounted for the largest share of assessments, while preventable image-acquisition errors (poor lighting: 42.0%; poor focus: 28.0%; motion blur: 18.0%) represented the primary modifiable determinants of failure. In the independent tertiary referral cohort - heavily enriched with malignant and diagnostically challenging lesions - exact Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic agreements were 54.4% and 70.6%, respectively. However, combining Top-3 agreement, correct broader disease-group assignment, and appropriate risk-based routing yielded a clinically useful triage outcome in 80.0% of cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted skin analysis provides clinically meaningful support for early risk stratification and patient referral when deployed as a clinical decision-support tool rather than an autonomous diagnostic system. Comprehensive evaluation of medical AI requires pairing conventional accuracy metrics with triage-oriented clinical endpoints and transparent RWE reporting.

items.title: Student perceptions of generative artificial intelligence in university education: a study using the ZMET technique

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction This study aims to analyse university students' perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in their academic education, exploring how they construct meaning around its use and how these representations influence notions of learning, authorship and critical literacy in higher education. Methods The sample comprised 20 students from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. The Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) was employed as a qualitative elicitation approach using images and metaphorical narratives, applied via a two-phase protocol: a) a pre-task involving the independent selection of seven images; and b) a guided elicitation phase, based on questions that explore the participant's perception through analogies, sensory contrasts and emotional narratives. Results Within this corpus, participants articulated ambivalent representations of GenAI through several distinct metaphorical configurations, including an “other” to which participants attribute agency (a silent companion or tutor) and a pragmatic cognitive extension valued for its efficiency. These representations highlight a reconfiguration of the relationship between students and processes of knowledge production, blurring traditional boundaries between technological assistance, collaboration and authorship. On an emotional level, some accounts represented GenAI as an emotional buffer, offering relief from academic overload; however, this relief coexists with ethical vigilance and unease about “crossing a line” in academic honesty, reflecting processes of negotiation over intellectual responsibility and the legitimate use of generative systems in educational contexts. Discussion Regarding institutional adaptation, metaphors of misalignment and accounts of GenAI bridging gaps in academic support point to perceived gaps in institutional guidance and to the importance of pedagogical mediation, including clearer approaches to teaching and assessment in a context where GenAI is already part of university life. Taken together, the accounts show how participants interpret GenAI as a context-specific form of academic support and guidance. These representations link the negotiation of trust and authorship to the perceived accessibility of university support, offering insights into critical literacy and institutional mediation.

The equal allocation across the four settings was defined in advance as a design quota, ensuring an equal contribution from each institutional context to the corpus. Because this quota was fixed before data collection, theoretical saturation was not used as the stopping rule for recruitment. The fixed sample therefore constituted the corpus for the interpretive analysis reported here. The study makes no claim to statistical representativeness or to national-level comparison. The four countries were those represented by the public universities participating in the COIL programme. The study was not designed as a cross-country comparison; rather, the inclusion of Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru made it possible to consider students' experiences across different university settings while keeping the disciplinary field broadly constant. The restriction to the field of Social Sciences was based on both feasibility criteria for conducting fieldwork and theoretical criteria, given that the social sciences are characterised by intensive use of academic writing, argumentation, critical reading and the production of reflective texts—practices in which GenAI plays a particularly significant and problematic role in terms of authorship, interpretation and epistemological judgement ( Fontanelli et al., 2025 ). Working within the same broad disciplinary field also reduced one source of variation across the corpus. The equal number of participants from each setting was intended to widen the range of university experiences represented, not to estimate national differences. Age, gender and country are reported only to provide context for the quotations and were not used to form analytic groups. A variant of the ZMET technique was used for data collection. The approach builds on the broader premise, central to conceptual metaphor theory, that metaphor helps structure how people understand and communicate experience ( ), and on ZMET's use of participant-selected images to elicit associations that may be difficult to formulate in direct questioning ( ). In this study, ZMET was used as an elicitation device rather than as a means of accessing a presumed “subconscious”. Since its development, ZMET has been widely used to explore consumer experiences, meanings and perceptions in marketing; however, its application has expanded to other research aims and disciplinary fields ( ). The data collection process was carried out in two phases per participant: Image Selection (Homework or Pre-task). Before the interview, each participant received a document outlining the study's aim, the procedure and informed consent process and was asked to independently select seven images representing GenAI in their academic experience. Images could be drawn from personal photographs, magazines or publicly available online material; no predefined image set was provided. Participants were asked not to enter the focal term, or an equivalent direct label, into a search engine in order to reduce direct lexical priming rather than to restrict the use of online sources. To support this phase, a dedicated website ( https://competenciamediatica.wixsite.com/zmet-ia ) was created, featuring an introductory video that briefly explains what is meant by GenAI. Participants were required to watch this video before selecting their images. The task was completed individually over approximately three days, after which the selected images were sent to the researcher by email. Their meaning was established through the participants’ subsequent explanations during the interview; therefore, images were not interpreted independently of the accompanying narratives. The video provided a general explanation of GenAI and included statements describing AI systems as capable of analysing, learning and acting autonomously. This framing formed part of the elicitation context; its potential influence is considered in the limitations. Elicitation or Guided Interview (ZMET Core). Semi-structured interviews were conducted in which participants verbally explained the relationship between each of the seven selected images and their perception of the GenAI, following the six-stage ZMET protocol ( Hancock and Miller, 2025 ). An interview guide comprising 16 open-ended questions was used for this process ( Table 1 ). During the interviews, probing techniques were employed to expand upon and clarify the emerging metaphorical narratives. The questions were designed to explore not only the uses attributed to the GenAI but also the representations linked to learning, authorship, academic relationships and institutional adaptation. Questions about sound, taste, texture, smell and colour formed part of the elicitation strategy. Sensory associations were considered alongside the explanations of the images and the narratives when they helped to clarify a metaphorical interpretation, without constituting independent categories. These positions could coexist within a single person's account. Previous studies have documented the perceived usefulness, concerns and academic uses of GenAI ( Álvarez-Hernández and Pérez-Velasco, 2025 ; Koohang et al., 2024 ). Metaphorical analysis enables us to understand how these experiences are organised, because seemingly similar uses take on different meanings depending on whether AI is viewed as a tool, a presence with which one converses, or an authority. And this distinction helps to explain why knowing the task performed is insufficient to understand how assistance and trust in the system are experienced. Symbolic authority makes this distinction particularly evident. Images of illuminated manuscripts, libraries and guiding lights were interpreted alongside accounts in which participants described GenAI as someone who “has already read everything” or as a source of explanations they trusted more than their own understanding of a lesson. These materials suggest that perceived clarity and the breadth of knowledge can become grounds for attributing credibility. In relation to debates on cognitive dependence and critical literacy ( Fernández-Prados et al., 2025 ; Marrone et al., 2025 ), the contribution lies in situating this trust within a specific interpretative relationship: a response may be accepted because it takes the place of an expert voice. The concern expressed in these accounts encompasses both the delegation of work and the possibility of accepting an error without acknowledging it. However, it is important to clarify the scope of this interpretation. The accounts allow us to examine how participants describe their trust; they do not enable us to establish the accuracy of the answers they used or to demonstrate an actual reduction in their autonomy of judgement. With regard to the second research question, the frameworks of the “emotional buffer”, “ethical traffic light” and “cognitive crutch” show how relief and concern can be intertwined in accounts of academic support. The emotional buffer represents a means of overcoming the difficulty of getting started. The “ethical traffic light” expresses uncertainty about the limits of acceptable assistance, whilst the “cognitive crutch” reflects the fear that such help may lead to dependency. These frameworks help us to understand the coexistence of benefits and risks described in previous research ( Blanc-Pihuave and Gil-Mateos, 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ): assistance can be experienced as a resource that enables progress whilst, at the same time, raising doubts about intellectual responsibility. The contrast drawn by one participant between essays largely produced using AI and a video task requiring filming and editing also suggests that the recognition of authorship may depend on the contribution the student considers significant. This account invites us to examine how the design of tasks influences the perceived boundary between assistance and substitution. It does not demonstrate that repetitive activities lead to the use of GenAI, nor that such uses preserve learning. The “masks of academic production” and “knowledge that leaves no trace” express two different concerns. The first reflects uncertainty about the relationship between the submitted text and the student's own contribution, even when the result appears to retain a recognisable personal style. The second, using the analogy of fast food, contrasts immediate utility with an understanding perceived as superficial. Reading them together allows us to distinguish between the concern for recognising one's own contribution and the concern for what has been learnt during the process. Obtaining a usable result, feeling that it is one's own, and perceiving that something has been learnt are experiences that do not necessarily coincide. The student profile configurations also help to answer the second question, as they illustrate different ways of approaching GenAI. The cartographer emphasises guidance and decision-making; the puppet raises the possibility of losing control; and the hybrid student represents the incorporation of technological assistance into academic practice. Within this corpus, autonomy and dependence are expressed as possibilities for retaining, sharing or relinquishing control, rather than as fixed types of students. Consequently, the hybrid configuration does not constitute proof that collaboration preserves intellectual agency. Read alongside the “puppet” and the “cognitive crutch”, it allows us to examine how that agency is negotiated without presupposing the outcome of the negotiation. items.title: Engage, understand, reflect, and learn: an exploratory qualitative study of AI-generated reflective visuals in students’ assessments

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-generated visuals are increasingly being explored in higher education as tools to support student learning and reflection, yet little is known about how students experience their use in reflective assessment. This qualitative study explored the experiences and perceptions of first-year students ( n = 10) using AI-generated reflective visuals (AIGRVs) as part of a reflective assessment approach in a general education course at a Middle Eastern university. The study analyzed students' open-ended survey responses thematically to understand how they described and made sense of creating, interpreting, and evaluating AI-generated visuals as part of their learning. Basic quantitative results from the same surveys, including responses to Likert-scale statements, were also analysed and used as supplementary evidence to support the qualitative findings. The analysis highlighted four interconnected areas: engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning. Students described using AIGRVs to represent and connect course concepts, evaluate AI-generated outputs, and reflect on their learning experiences. The quantitative data were consistent with these accounts but were interpreted cautiously because of the very small samples. Overall, the study offers preliminary, context-specific insights into how AIGRVs may function as cognitive and metacognitive scaffolds within reflective assessment and identifies directions for larger and more rigorous studies.

reading.interpretation: This exploratory qualitative study sought to understand how first-year students described their experiences with AI-generated reflective visuals in course assessments. The discussion is guided by the research question: In what ways do AI-generated visuals support students’ engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning? Students’ qualitative accounts portrayed the AIGRV tasks as enjoyable, interactive, memorable, and easier to connect with, suggesting that engagement stemmed from active involvement in creating and interpreting the visuals. This interpretation aligns with studies reporting engagement benefits when AI-generated visuals are meaningfully integrated into learning activities ( Bian et al., 2025 ; Dakamsih et al., 2025 ; Granström and Oppi, 2025 ; Shi et al., 2024 ). The findings indicate how these students perceived engagement with AIGRVs rather than demonstrating that AIGRVs increase engagement relative to traditional assessment methods. Kolb’s (1984) experiential learning cycle offers a useful interpretive lens for the assignment design: students engaged with an experience or problem, reflected on it, connected the experience to course concepts, and considered application or revision. However, the study did not directly observe or measure students’ progression through all four stages of Kolb's cycle. The findings therefore indicate alignment between assignment elements and the theory, rather than empirical confirmation of a complete developmental progression. One notable finding of this study was the perceived role of AIGRVs in supporting students’ conceptual understanding. analysis.methods: This study used an exploratory qualitative design, with students’ open-ended survey responses as the primary evidence. The design was selected because the study sought to understand how first-year university students described and made meaning of their experiences of creating AI-generated reflective visuals (AIGRVs) as part of course assessments. The qualitative analysis focused on students’ accounts of engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning. The study also collected quantitative data from survey statements as supplementary descriptive data to support the qualitative findings. Participants were first-year undergraduate students enrolled on the Strategic Learning and Growth course at a large public university in the Middle East. Ten students were enrolled in the course, and all ten participated in this research. They came from four main disciplines: three students in computational systems, three in business transformation, two in interior design, and two in social innovation. The researchers developed two surveys to collect qualitative and quantitative data. Survey 1 consisted of five open-ended questions inviting written reflections on students’ experiences, challenges, and suggestions: How did using AI-generated reflective visuals impact your engagement with the course material? Please explain with an example. Can you describe a specific instance where AI visuals helped you better understand a concept or topic? Can you describe a specific instance where AI visuals helped you better understand a concept or topic? What challenges did you face while using AI-generated visuals, and how do you think these could be addressed? In what ways would you like to see AI-generated visuals integrated into other assessments or class activities? The survey also included demographic and contextual questions, along with 20 Likert-type statements organized around engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning. Survey 2 also included three sections. Section asked students to share an AIGRV they had generated. Section consisted of three open-ended questions to prompt reflection on their AI-generated visual: Reflect on this visual. In what way does it reflect your own learning this semester? Please explain with examples. Critically analyze this visual: What aspects could be improved, what elements are missing, and what suggestions do you have to enhance its overall effectiveness and clarity? What insights or key takeaways have you gained from this visual? How does it contribute to your understanding of the topic? also included three 5-point Likert-scale questions exploring the extent to which students perceived that they had met the course learning outcomes. To support content validity, other faculty members familiar with the course reviewed the survey questions for clarity, relevance, and alignment with the study aims and learning outcomes. The authors used their feedback to refine the questions before administration. Before data collection, the authors explained the study to the students during class, including its purpose, aims, and the steps involved in participation. Students were informed about what they would be asked to complete and how their responses would contribute to a better understanding of the use of AI-generated reflective visuals in learning and assessment. It was clearly explained that participation was entirely voluntary, that choosing not to participate would not affect their grades or course experience, and that their responses would remain confidential. Students were also informed that their contributions could add value to existing knowledge and help improve understanding of how AI-generated visuals may support students’ learning experiences. The researchers followed the procedures outlined below: Students first completed the relevant course learning activities and then completed assignments 1 and 2, which required them to create, interpret, and reflect on AI-generated visuals. After completing Assignment 2, students were invited to participate in Survey 1. Survey 1 was administered via Google Forms. Students completed the Likert-scale and open-ended questions about their experiences with AIGRVs. Ten students completed the survey. Students continued to use AI-generated visuals in the subsequent course assessment 3. After students completed the final assessment (Assignment 4), they were invited to complete Survey 2, which was also administered via Google Forms. Survey 2 asked students to reflect on their overall learning experience and to evaluate their use of AI-generated visuals. Four students completed this survey. Survey 2 received fewer responses because it was administered during the final week of the semester. Many students no longer attended classes regularly or checked their university email after submitting their final assignments, making further follow-up with students very limited. The analysis was primarily qualitative. Open-ended responses from both surveys were analyzed thematically to identify recurring meanings in students’ descriptions of their engagement with AIGRVs, their understanding of course concepts, their reflective processes, and their perceived learning. Thematic analysis followed Braun and Clarke’s (2022) approach. The four study concepts—engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning—provided an initial organizing framework, and coding within these areas remained attentive to recurring meanings and examples in students’ accounts. The researchers repeatedly read the responses, generated and compared codes across participants, refined patterns of meaning, and selected quotations that illustrated both common and contrasting experiences. Ten students ( n = 10) completed the first survey, and four students ( n = 4) completed the second. Across the open-ended questions, a total of 50 responses were collected from Survey 1 and 12 from Survey 2. The total number of words was 2032, with individual responses ranging from 1 to 241 words. The average length of each response was 41 words with a median of 18 words. Although some responses were brief, others offered more detailed reflections and examples. Responses to the Likert-scale survey statements were analyzed using Excel. Means and were calculated for each statement and used to provide supplementary evidence rather than to validate or statistically triangulate the themes. This approach keeps the students’ accounts central to interpretation while allowing the small numerical dataset to show whether the direction of the responses to the statements were broadly consistent with those accounts. Ethical approval was obtained
analysis.results: This section presents the qualitative findings as the primary evidence for understanding students’ experiences with AIGRVs. The findings are organized around engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning, with students’ accounts and illustrative quotations forming the basis for interpretation. Descriptive Likert-scale patterns are included within each area as supplementary evidence. Student responses on engagement indicate that using AIGRVs made their learning process more engaging. Students noted that creating the visual representation in the assignment helped them sustain attention and engagement: “Learning with AI visuals feels more engaging and easier to understand than traditional methods… the visuals helped me see the concept in action.” (Alya, Survey 1). As a result, “AI visuals made learning more interactive and memorable compared to traditional text-based methods, which can feel passive and harder to retain.” (Ahmed, Survey 1). Several factors contributed to this enhanced engagement. First, “Using AI-generated reflective visuals significantly enhanced my engagement with the course material by making abstract concepts more concrete and personally relatable.” (Omar, Survey 1). Second, AIGRVs were “easier to connect with than traditional methods” (Alya, Survey 1). Overall, most students used terms such as fun, easier, more interesting, engaging, and more experiential, and perceived AIGRVs as tools that increased their engagement and made their assignments more interesting and stimulating. The quantitative findings showed generally positive engagement with AIGRVs (M = 4.30, n = 10,). See Tables 2 , 7 for details. Survey statements for engagement - survey 1 ( n = 10). Students perceived AIGRVs as an effective way of communicating their understanding of the course material. One student explained how AIGRVs helped transform abstract ideas into concrete and memorable representations: “A specific instance where AI visuals helped me better understand a concept was during a lesson on the growth mindset. The AI generated an image comparing two brains: one labeled “Fixed Mindset,” shown as a rigid maze with dead ends, and the other labeled “Growth Mindset,” portrayed as a tree with branching paths and new buds. This visual made it immediately clear how a fixed mindset can limit progress, while a growth mindset allows for continuous development and exploration. Seeing that contrast visually helped me internalize the idea much more effectively than just reading about it.” (Omar, Survey 1). Students frequently described how AI visuals allowed them to clarify complex or abstract ideas and make them more personalized and relatable. For example, one student explained: “When studying emotional agility, the AI visualized my emotional journey through a week of academic stress as a winding path with different weather patterns—sunny for confident moments, cloudy for uncertainty, and stormy for anxiety. This image helped me better understand how my emotions shifted over time and how I could respond more flexibly to challenges.” (Omar, Survey 1) This idea was complemented by another student who explained how using AI visuals enhanced the learning process: “Using AI-generated reflective visuals helped me understand the course material better by showing ideas in a clear and creative way. For example, when we were learning about contrast, I used AI to create an image that showed light and dark shapes together. This helped me see how contrast works and gave me ideas for my own project.” (Rashid, Survey 1) The quantitative responses in Table 3 also suggest that students perceived AIGRVs as effective in communicating their understanding of course material and concepts. Survey statements for conceptual understanding - survey 1 ( n = 10). AIGRVs supported critical reflection in two main ways. First, the very act of creating them encouraged students to reflect rather than just completing the task: for example, “I became more aware of how I was feeling and how to work through it. I didn't just force myself to finish things. I started to reflect, adjust, and focus better.” (Noor, Survey 2). In particular, the AI-generated visual encouraged students to think more deeply about their own behavior. One student described the visual they had generated: “Climbing a staircase while distractions pulled at them made the struggle more tangible and emotionally resonant. This helped me reflect more deeply on my own habits and solutions.” (Rashid, Survey 1). It also enabled them to see and understand their learning journey and progress: “It helped me see how much I’ve changed in a short time. It shows that growth takes small steps, like improving habits and confidence. It made me realise how my mindset and actions affect my learning. It also reminded me that challenges helped me become stronger and more focused.” (Omar, Survey 2) Second, prompting the AI tool to generate the image or visual was central to this critical reflection. This prompting was often driven by dissatisfaction with the initial image they created: “A lot of times, the images would be of poor quality and/or not cover the material correctly, and they would need editing.” (Hessa, Survey 1). Students were also quite specific about the weaknesses in their initial visual (see the student's AIGRV in Figure 2 ): Example of student AIGRV showing how the student used critical reflection to enhance her visual. “The visual shows my growth clearly, but it can be better. It needs labels like “before” and “now” to show the steps. Adding small icons or drawings can help people understand it faster. Also, using arrows or a timeline would show my progress more clearly. It's nice, but these changes would make it easier to follow.” (Alya, Survey 2) This dissatisfaction often pushed students to reflect on and refine the description of the image they wanted by iterating the prompts, so that the resulting images better represented their learning journey: “Some AI algorithms would need some tweaking in order to get a coherent image. analysis.discussion: This exploratory qualitative study sought to understand how first-year students described their experiences with AI-generated reflective visuals in course assessments. The discussion is guided by the research question: In what ways do AI-generated visuals support students’ engagement, conceptual understanding, critical reflection, and learning? Students’ qualitative accounts portrayed the AIGRV tasks as enjoyable, interactive, memorable, and easier to connect with, suggesting that engagement stemmed from active involvement in creating and interpreting the visuals. This interpretation aligns with studies reporting engagement benefits when AI-generated visuals are meaningfully integrated into learning activities ( Bian et al., 2025 ; Dakamsih et al., 2025 ; Granström and Oppi, 2025 ; Shi et al., 2024 ). The findings indicate how these students perceived engagement with AIGRVs rather than demonstrating that AIGRVs increase engagement relative to traditional assessment methods. Kolb’s (1984) experiential learning cycle offers a useful interpretive lens for the assignment design: students engaged with an experience or problem, reflected on it, connected the experience to course concepts, and considered application or revision. However, the study did not directly observe or measure students’ progression through all four stages of Kolb's cycle. The findings therefore indicate alignment between assignment elements and the theory, rather than empirical confirmation of a complete developmental progression. One notable finding of this study was the perceived role of AIGRVs in supporting students’ conceptual understanding. Rather than viewing the visuals as merely creative outputs, students described them as tools that helped them better understand course concepts, recognize relationships between ideas, organize information more effectively, and develop a clearer understanding of complex topics, such as executive functions ( Bian et al., 2025 ; Huh et al., 2025 ; Yuan and Hu, 2024 ). This suggests that AIGRVs helped students build meaningful representations of their knowledge, moving them beyond recalling isolated facts toward a more integrated understanding of course content. The cognitive processes involved in creating the visuals were also prominent ( de Souza et al., 2024 ; Fiorella, 2023 ; Fiorella and Mayer, 2015 ; Nieto-Leal et al., 2026 ). Developing an AI-generated reflective image required students to first identify the key concepts from the course material, determine how these concepts related to one another, organize them into a coherent structure, and then translate abstract ideas into visual representations through carefully designed prompts ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yuan and Hu, 2024 ). This process required students to make deliberate decisions about what was most important, how ideas connected, and how complex concepts could be represented in meaningful ways, a process that facilitates deeper understanding and meaningful learning experiences ( de Souza et al., 2024 ; Nieto-Leal et al., 2026 ; Yuan and Hu, 2024 ). Consequently, the learning process extended beyond memorization or content reproduction, requiring students to actively construct, reorganize, and synthesize their knowledge before producing a visual representation, thereby enhancing students’ motivation and knowledge integration ( Chen et al., 2025 ). These findings align with Dual Coding Theory ( Paivio, 1990 ), which holds that learning is strengthened when information is processed through both verbal and visual channels. By transforming written reflections into AIGRVs, students engaged multiple representational systems, potentially strengthening cognitive connections among concepts and improving recall and understanding ( Nieto-Leal et al., 2026 ). This study also contributes to the broader literature on AIGVCs in higher education. While previous studies have reported that AI-generated images can increase engagement, motivation, and creativity (e.g., Chen and Lin, 2024 ; Huh et al., 2025 ), the present study suggests that their educational value extends beyond these outcomes. Students perceived the process of generating reflective visuals as helping them integrate ideas, recognize conceptual relationships, and make abstract concepts more accessible ( Tlili et al., 2023 ). This suggests that AIGRVs should be viewed not merely as innovative technological products but as pedagogical tools that can facilitate conceptual understanding by encouraging students to organize, interpret, and reconstruct knowledge. Rather than replacing learning, AIGRVs appear to support deeper cognitive engagement by making students active participants in constructing meaning ( Vygotsky, 1978 ). Across the qualitative accounts, students linked creating visuals with organizing, clarifying, and representing course concepts, a pattern also supported by the descriptive quantitative findings. This process aligns with Kolb’s (1984) abstract conceptualization, as students connected their experiences with course concepts and translated abstract ideas into visual representations. It also reflects Schön’s (1983) reflective practice, as evaluating and refining the visuals encouraged students to reconsider and clarify their understanding. Thus, creating and reflecting on AIGRVs may support conceptual understanding by helping students organize knowledge and make connections among ideas ( Chi and Wylie, 2014 ; Kahu, 2013 ; Kahu and Nelson, 2018 ). Students described AIGRVs as supporting their critical reflection by prompting them to actively examine and evaluate their learning throughout the visual creation process. Rather than simply recalling information and producing an AI-generated image with the first prompt, students were required to engage in a reflective process; to reflect on what they had learned, identify the most significant concepts, determine how these ideas were connected, consider how their understanding could be represented visually, compose an initial prompt, judge the accuracy and relevance of the generated visuals, and refine both the prompts and the final image. In doing so, students continually questioned whether the generated images accurately reflected their understanding and whether alternative representations could better communicate the relationships among concepts. The educational value of the activity, therefore, lay not in the AI-generated image itself but in the critical reflection required to create, interpret, and refine it. In addition, AI served as a cognitive partner that stimulated questioning, evaluation, and refinement rather than replacing students’ intellectual effort. The finding challenges concerns that gener
analysis.limitations: Given the small, self-selected sample and the absence of a comparison condition, these findings should be understood as context-specific and exploratory, providing a foundation for larger qualitative, mixed-methods, and experimental studies. Several limitations shape the interpretation of this exploratory qualitative study. First, the primary qualitative evidence came from a very small sample in one first-year course at a single Middle Eastern institution, while the supplementary quantitative evidence involved only 10 participants in Survey 1 and four in Survey 2. The findings are therefore context-specific and intended for analytical insight rather than statistical generalization. Second, the study relied on self-reported survey responses rather than interviews or extended qualitative narratives; the depth of the qualitative evidence is consequently limited. Students’ perceptions may also be influenced by their cultural, educational, and institutional environment; therefore, their experiences may differ from those of students in other countries or university settings. items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can support university learning, yet psychological reliance on AI-generated feedback may limit independent mastery experiences. Under an integrated I-PACE–social cognitive framework, this three-wave observational study examined whether self-efficacy for learning and performance statistically accounted for the association between AI dependence and subsequent academic engagement, and whether physical activity moderated the first-stage association. The analysis was based on 1,068 quality-screened students matched across baseline (T1), Week 4 (T2), and Week 8 (T3) questionnaires. AI dependence and physical activity were measured at T1, self-efficacy at T1/T2, and academic engagement at T1/T3. Standardized regression-based PROCESS Models 4 and 7 adjusted for baseline self-efficacy and engagement, demographics, and AI-use intensity. Higher T1 AI dependence was associated with lower T2 self-efficacy ( β = −0.137), while T2 self-efficacy was positively associated with T3 engagement ( β = 0.114). The first-stage interaction was small ( β = 0.073; ΔR 2 = 0.005), with an index of moderated mediation of 0.008 (5,000-resample 95% bootstrap CI [0.002, 0.017]). Inverse-probability-of-completion weighting produced similar core estimates; longitudinal measurement-invariance and latent autoregressive SEM results are additionally reported as sensitivity evidence. The results identify a short-term, temporally ordered indirect association involving academic self-efficacy, not an established causal mechanism. Educators may preserve students’ independent mastery opportunities when designing AI-assisted coursework.

Baseline univariate differences between final completers and other eligible T1 respondents were generally small ( Table 1 ). reading.interpretation: This three-wave study tested a temporally ordered pathway from AI dependence to later academic engagement through self-efficacy for learning and performance, with physical activity as a first-stage boundary condition. The primary PROCESS analysis supported the proposed indirect association and a small moderation effect. Longitudinal scalar invariance was supported for self-efficacy and engagement, the core pattern was robust to omission of either age or grade, and an inverse-probability-weighted sensitivity analysis yielded similar estimates. The latent-variable autoregressive SEM likewise reproduced the core indirect pathway after explicitly modeling measurement error and baseline stability. Accordingly, the main inferences are best interpreted as short-term longitudinal associations rather than causal effects. The prospective association between AI dependence and lower subsequent self-efficacy is consistent with the integrated I-PACE–social cognitive framework. I-PACE highlights how repeated reliance can become reinforced through affective relief, cognitive expectations, and control processes ( Brand et al., 2019 ), whereas social cognitive theory identifies mastery experience as a central source of self-efficacy ( Bandura, 1986 ; Bandura, 1997 ). In the present context, students who repeatedly require AI-generated confirmation may complete tasks efficiently while obtaining less direct evidence that they can solve the same problems independently. This interpretation differs from claiming that AI use itself is detrimental. AI-use frequency and duration were controlled, and the focal construct was psychological dependence rather than exposure. analysis.methods: This study used a three-wave longitudinal survey design among university students recruited from universities in two cities in central China and one university in Northeast China. Data were collected across three waves in 2026 at approximately monthly intervals within a single academic period. No universal time lag is optimal for longitudinal mediation; the interval was selected to provide temporal separation between predictor, mediator, and outcome assessments while maintaining a short-term follow-up window and limiting loss to follow-up, consistent with recommendations that lag selection should reflect the process under study rather than a fixed statistical rule ( Cole and Maxwell, 2003 ). At T1, participants completed AI dependence, physical activity, baseline self-efficacy, baseline academic engagement, AI-use variables, and demographic variables. T2 reassessed self-efficacy and AI-use frequency, and T3 reassessed academic engagement and AI-use frequency. Participants used a self-generated six-character anonymous code at all three waves to permit linkage without collecting names or student numbers. The T1 dataset contained 2,018 responses. Prespecified quality screening excluded respondents who did not provide consent, failed the instructed-response attention check, completed the baseline questionnaire in less than 180 s, had missing core variables, or gave logically inconsistent responses indicating no AI use while simultaneously reporting nonzero AI-use frequency or duration. Attention checks and response-time screening were used as complementary indicators of careless or insufficient-effort responding ( Meade and Craig, 2012 ). After screening, 1,762 participants remained in the eligible T1 cohort. The T2 survey yielded 1,671 responses, of which 1,571 passed the attention check; the T3 survey yielded 1,421 responses, of which 1,308 passed the attention check. After anonymous-code matching and wave-specific quality screening, 1,068 participants formed the primary complete-case analytic sample. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xinjiang Normal University (approval number: XJNU2026LLSC52). All participants provided informed consent before completing the survey. The surveys were anonymous, and matching across waves was conducted using participant-generated anonymous codes. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. AI dependence was assessed at T1 using a Chinese learning-context-adapted version of the five-item Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale (DAI-5) developed by Morales-García et al. (2024) . The original scale was developed as a unidimensional measure of perceived dependence on AI among university students. Items were rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The adaptation retained the five conceptual domains while contextualizing wording to academic tasks; for example, one item asked whether the student needed AI feedback or confirmation to feel more confident when completing learning or decision-related tasks. Higher mean scores indicated greater AI dependence. The original study supported a one-factor structure, and internal consistency in the present sample was α = 0.933. The Chinese wording was adapted for the learning context while preserving the conceptual content of the original five items. Self-efficacy was assessed at T1 and T2 using the eight-item self-efficacy for learning and performance subscale of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) ( Pintrich et al., 1991 ). analysis.discussion: This three-wave study tested a temporally ordered pathway from AI dependence to later academic engagement through self-efficacy for learning and performance, with physical activity as a first-stage boundary condition. The primary PROCESS analysis supported the proposed indirect association and a small moderation effect. Longitudinal scalar invariance was supported for self-efficacy and engagement, the core pattern was robust to omission of either age or grade, and an inverse-probability-weighted sensitivity analysis yielded similar estimates. The latent-variable autoregressive SEM likewise reproduced the core indirect pathway after explicitly modeling measurement error and baseline stability. Accordingly, the main inferences are best interpreted as short-term longitudinal associations rather than causal effects. The prospective association between AI dependence and lower subsequent self-efficacy is consistent with the integrated I-PACE–social cognitive framework. I-PACE highlights how repeated reliance can become reinforced through affective relief, cognitive expectations, and control processes ( Brand et al., 2019 ), whereas social cognitive theory identifies mastery experience as a central source of self-efficacy ( Bandura, 1986 ; Bandura, 1997 ). In the present context, students who repeatedly require AI-generated confirmation may complete tasks efficiently while obtaining less direct evidence that they can solve the same problems independently. This interpretation differs from claiming that AI use itself is detrimental. AI-use frequency and duration were controlled, and the focal construct was psychological dependence rather than exposure. The result therefore aligns more closely with recent work distinguishing productive AI use from problematic or dependent use ( Zhang and Xu, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Morales-García et al., 2024 ; Jia et al., 2025 ) than with a simple “more AI is worse” account. Self-efficacy, in turn, prospectively predicted academic engagement even after baseline engagement was controlled. This finding is consistent with social cognitive accounts in which perceived capability supports persistence, effort, and willingness to remain engaged when tasks become difficult ( Bandura, 1986 ; Bandura, 1997 ; Zimmerman, 2000 ; Pajares, 1996 ; Honicke and Broadbent, 2016 ; Richardson et al., 2012 ; Schunk, 1991 ; Pintrich et al., 1991 ; Pintrich, 2003 ). The latent SEM strengthened this interpretation because the AI dependence-to-self-efficacy and self-efficacy-to-engagement paths remained after measurement error and autoregressive stability were modeled. The study therefore adds a temporal element to prior cross-sectional evidence: self-efficacy is not merely correlated with both AI dependence and engagement at the same occasion, but can statistically account for part of the short-term association over the short follow-up. Nevertheless, because AI dependence was not repeatedly measured, the design cannot rule out reciprocal or unmeasured third-variable processes. Physical activity modestly attenuated the association between AI dependence and subsequent self-efficacy. This result is compatible with evidence linking physical activity with cognitive, affective, and self-regulatory functioning ( Bull et al., 2020 ; World Health Organization, 2020 ; Lubans et al., 2016 ; Biddle and Asare, 2011 ; Kandola et al., 2019 ; Rebar et al., 2015 ; Schuch et al., 2018 ; Stubbs et al., 2018 ; Liang, 1994 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) and with studies in which physical activity operates as a moderator of psychological risk pathways ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2025a , b , c , d ; Jiang et al., 2022 ). Within the present framework, activity may provide non-digital mastery experiences, behavioral activation, and affect-regulatory resources that help preserve perceived capability. However, the interaction explained only ΔR 2 = 0.005, and the high-activity conditional indirect effect included zero. Physical activity should therefore be interpreted as a modest boundary condition, not as a treatment for AI dependence or as a substitute for instructional design. The questionnaires did not directly assess exercise-related mastery transfer, emotion regulation, or a specific embodied self-regulatory construct. Accordingly, these are untested explanations, and the PARS-3 score should be interpreted only as the observed physical-activity rating.

items.title: Nurse–patient communication when patients introduce AI-generated health information: a qualitative study of clinical nurses’ experiences and responses

items.abstract_text: Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly becomes a source of health information for patients, some patients and family members have already obtained relevant explanations or recommendations from AI and brought this information into clinical communication. This change may create new communication demands for nurses. This study aimed to explore clinical nurses’ communication experiences and response strategies when patients or family members introduced AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. Using purposive sampling combined with a maximum variation strategy, 18 clinical nurses with relevant communication experience were recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China. One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted between May and August 2026. The interviews focused on specific nurse–patient communication events personally experienced by the participants. Data were analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results Two themes and six subthemes were identified. The first theme, changes in nurse–patient communication in the context of AI, included seeking confirmation from or questioning nurses using AI-generated health information, increased explanatory work, and increased communication opportunities. The second theme, nurses’ responses to AI-generated health information, included identifying patients’ actual concerns, explaining information differences in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and maintaining communication while seeking professional support. Conclusion The introduction of AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication may both increase nurses’ explanatory work and create new opportunities for communication. Nurses may need to consider patients’ existing understanding and actual concerns, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and clinical arrangements in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and seek professional support when necessary. These findings may inform efforts to support nurses’ communication skills, although their applicability across different clinical settings requires further exploration.

reading.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, all participants were female nurses recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China, which may limit the transferability of the findings to other healthcare settings and regions. Second, the findings were based on nurses’ retrospective accounts and may have been affected by recall and social desirability bias. Purposive sampling was used to recruit nurses who met the inclusion criteria, together with a maximum variation strategy to capture a range of experiences across different care contexts. Variation was sought primarily in clinical department, years of nursing experience, and the types of AI-related nurse–patient communication events experienced by participants. Recruitment information was distributed through hospital nursing administration departments or designated departmental contacts, and interested nurses contacted the research team directly. The researchers conducted a brief screening to confirm participants’ relevant experiences. Eligible nurses were then informed about the study purpose, interview procedures, and intended use of the data and were free to decide whether to participate. A total of 21 nurses volunteered for the study. To maintain variation across clinical departments, three volunteers (two from internal medicine and one from surgery) were not selected for the final sample because these departments were already represented among the selected participants. A total of 18 nurses were included in the study. Sample adequacy was assessed with reference to the concept of information power, taking into account the specificity of the research question, the relevance of participants’ experiences to the research question, the richness of the interview data, and the degree of experiential variation required for the analysis ( 20 ). Data richness was assessed based on the specificity of communication events, the contextual details provided, and nurses’ descriptions of their judgments and responses. Data collection and preliminary analysis proceeded concurrently, allowing the research team to assess whether the accounts provided sufficient depth and variation to address the research question. Sample adequacy was therefore considered in relation to the depth and diversity of the accounts rather than a predetermined numerical threshold. The 18 interviews provided detailed accounts of specific nurse–patient communication events and variation in participants’ clinical backgrounds and experiences. analysis.discussion: After patients obtain health information through AI, nurse–patient communication may extend beyond nurses simply providing explanations and guidance to include confirming patients’ existing understanding and comparing information from different sources. Nurses may need to address discrepancies between AI-generated health information and actual clinical arrangements, while also making use of patients’ prior knowledge and proactively raised questions to facilitate communication. Understanding patients’ underlying concerns, assessing the applicability of AI-generated health information to the individual clinical situation, and seeking additional professional support when uncertainty arises emerged as important components of nurse–patient communication in this context. Patients’ use of AI to obtain health information before communicating with nurses allows them to enter clinical conversations with pre-existing understanding, seek confirmation from nurses, or compare AI-generated recommendations with actual clinical arrangements. Tan et al. ( 7 ) reported that patients may bring health information obtained from the internet into clinical encounters and verify their existing understanding by asking questions or discussing the information with healthcare professionals. Similarly, a survey of respondents in the United States by Ayo-Ajibola et al. ( 1 ) found that some patients considered treatment options based on information generated by ChatGPT while also seeking further confirmation from physicians. Previous studies have examined the influence of AI-generated health information on patient education and the professional role of nurses. The present study extends this work by focusing specifically on situations in which patients or family members actively introduce AI-generated health information into everyday nurse–patient communication. It illustrates how nurses respond to patients’ existing understanding, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and actual clinical arrangements, and experience changes in their communication work during this process. However, patients’ prior access to health information does not necessarily mean that nurses will always face a greater explanatory burden. Some nurses in this study noted that when patients had already acquired relevant basic knowledge or used AI to organize the questions they wanted to ask, the discussion could move directly to issues related to the patient’s specific situation. Liu et al. ( 10 ) similarly found that AI chatbots may facilitate patients’ access to health knowledge, while the generated content may also increase the explanatory work required of nurses. In a study of patient interactions with a GPT-4 chatbot, Carl et al. ( 21 ) found that most patients perceived the information provided as useful, comprehensive, and easy to understand, although they still placed greater value on clinicians’ explanations of medical issues. The authors also suggested that if AI can provide some preliminary explanations, it may allow healthcare professionals to devote more time to more complex concerns ( 21 ). These findings suggest that the influence of AI-generated health information on nurse–patient communication is not unidirectional, but may depend on the content of the information patients obtain, how they understand it, and how they express their concerns. When the information patients bring is complex or differs from actual clinical arrangements, nurses may need to spend additional time explaining these discrepancies. In contrast, when patients are able to articulate their concerns clearly, AI-generated health information may provide a useful basis for further discussion. Therefore, rather than focusing solely on whether patients use AI, it may be useful to examine how patients interpret and use AI-generated health information and how this information may shape the process of nurse–patient communication. From a precision health perspective, these findings suggest that the value of digital health information depends not only on its accessibility but also on how it is interpreted in relation to individual patients’ concerns and circumstances. Although AI-generated health information may not contain obvious errors, this does not mean that it can be directly applied to an individual patient. In this study, some nurses felt that explaining why generally correct information was not applicable to a particular patient was more difficult than correcting information that was clearly inaccurate. For example, patients might attribute their current discomfort to a medication after reading AI-generated health information about possible adverse effects and then ask whether the medication could be discontinued. In such situations, the key issue lies not only in whether the information provided by AI is factually correct, but also in how patients relate that information to their own symptoms and current treatment. Previous studies have also highlighted the limitations of AI-generated medical information. Wang et al. ( 22 ) noted that AI shows potential in providing general medical knowledge, but its reliability remains limited in more complex healthcare tasks. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Wei et al. ( 23 ) found substantial heterogeneity in the accuracy of ChatGPT responses to medical questions, with evaluation outcomes influenced by factors such as question type and assessment methods. While these studies have primarily focused on the accuracy of AI-generated health information, the present study further suggests, from the perspective of nurse–patient communication, that whether information is correct and whether it is applicable to a particular patient are two distinct issues that nurses need to consider separately. Participants noted that even when AI-generated content had a reasonable medical basis, patients could still develop inappropriate interpretations of their symptoms or clinical care arrangements if they overlooked the conditions under which the information was applicable. Therefore, when responding to AI-generated health information provided by patients, nurses may need to consider more than whether the information is correct or incorrect. They may also need to consider the patient’s condition, medication use, and stage of treatment, and explain the conditions under which the relevant recommendations may apply and how they differ from actual clinical arrangements. analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, all participants were female nurses recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China, which may limit the transferability of the findings to other healthcare settings and regions. Second, the findings were based on nurses’ retrospective accounts and may have been affected by recall and social desirability bias. The absence of direct observations and patient perspectives also limited a comprehensive understanding of nurse–patient communication. Third, organizational factors, including workload, staffing levels, time pressure, and hospital policies on AI use, were not examined. In addition, the versions and interfaces of AI tools were not recorded, and patients’ health and digital literacy and nurses’ AI literacy were not assessed. Finally, online interviews may have provided fewer observable nonverbal cues than face-to-face interviews, potentially affecting data richness. Future research should include diverse healthcare settings and both patient and nurse perspectives, incorporate direct observations, and examine how organizational factors, AI tool characteristics, and the health, digital, and AI literacy of patients and nurses shape nurse–patient communication.
