items.title: Emotionally Aware AI Chatbots for Adolescents: A Review of Psychological Principles for Learning, Calibrated Trust, and Healthy Human–AI Interaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.title: Generative AI adoption in organizations: A conceptual model of job crafting, employee productivity, creativity and work engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. It also provides managerial guidance for organizations that want GenAI adoption to deliver sustainable gains in performance and well being rather than short lived efficiency gains that erode over time.

items.title: Personalized AI-Supported Sport and Physical Activity for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Human Performance
items.abstract_text: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Engineering Sustainability
items.abstract_text: Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital twins (DTs) are increasingly promoted for sustainable built asset management, there is limited empirical evidence of their full lifecycle application – particularly in emerging economy contexts that combine technical, environmental, and human-centric performance indicators. This study examines the integration of an AI-enabled DT system across the design, construction, and operational stages of ‘Nirmitee Tower’, a green-certified commercial complex developed by a mid-sized construction firm in Central India. Adopting a mixed-methods case study approach, the research collected triangulated evidence from system analytics, environmental performance metrics, semi-structured interviews, and post-occupancy surveys. Operational definitions were applied for key measures such as material waste, comfort score, and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning energy use, with baselines drawn from comparable pre-DT projects. Key findings include: a 21% reduction in project delivery time, a 35.9% decrease in material waste, a 28.3% reduction in annual energy use, a 21.1% reduction in water consumption, and a 32% improvement in occupant comfort scores. This study contributes by providing a validated, multi-dimensional assessment framework for AI–DT performance, by demonstrating a rare emerging market case of full lifecycle DT integration in a small- and medium-scale enterprise context, and by aligning technical results with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 13).

items.title: Family, Psychotherapy, and AI: The Elephant in the Room

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming both personal and professional life. In this exploratory study, we investigate the potential role of AI in psychotherapy, focusing on systemic family therapy. We designed a simulation in which psychotherapists interacted with ChatGPT in a role-play scenario involving a distressed couple with a young child. Post-session interviews were held to assess participants’ perceptions of empathy, authenticity, risks, and professional implications. Our findings reveal that while AI can simulate empathy and facilitate useful reflection, it lacks the embodied relational presence crucial to therapy. In this article, we first discuss these results in relation to relevant literature on psychotherapy, technology, and AI. We then introduce a theoretical discussion, drawing on Bowen’s theory of emotional triangles, to speculate about the potential of new, implicit or explicit “technosocial triangles” among humans, therapists, and AIs. While this is a hypothesis rather than an empirical conclusion of our study, we argue that Bowen’s framework helps us imagine how AI might reshape relational systems in families and therapy.

items.venue: Journal of Accounting, Business and Management (JABM)
items.abstract_text: This study examines the extent to which AACSB-accredited accounting programs in the United States are integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into their curricula in response to evolving professional and technological demands. Using data from 184 AACSB-accredited institutions, we examine the presence of AI-focused degree programs and dedicated courses at both undergraduate and graduate levels. Our results indicate that, overall, AI adoption remains limited, with only 23.91% of programs offering specialized AI accounting degrees, 18.47% providing undergraduate AI accounting courses, and 22.28% including graduate-level AI accounting courses. Specialized degree programs lead slightly among adopters than graduate courses. AI integration typically occurs in isolated offerings rather than being embedded across curricula. Private institutions, although fewer in number, demonstrate proportionally higher adoption rates than public institutions. These findings highlight a potential gap between industry expectations for accounting graduates in terms of their level of readiness to utilize AI in their roles. These results suggest that accounting programs should strategically plan and integrate AI into their education to enhance student preparedness and professional relevance.

items.title: Application of an AI-powered virtual simulation combined with case-based learning in undergraduate emergency medicine education: focusing on advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Traditional lecture-based teaching has limitations in developing students' advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). This study primarily aimed to investigate whether the integrated AI-powered virtual simulation combined with CBL could improve students' higher-order clinical competencies and clinical transfer ability, and secondarily to obtain empirical evidence to support the optimization of undergraduate emergency medicine teaching. Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. Results Compared with the control group, the students in the experimental group demonstrated significant advantages in all assessment dimensions, including theoretical test, various practical skills in OSCE, disease assessment, emergency management, clinical decision-making, as well as learning confidence, autonomous learning ability and teaching satisfaction ( P &lt; 0.001). Further analysis indicated that within the experimental group, greater investment in study time was significantly associated with better clinical performance and diagnostic accuracy. Crucially, Cox regression analysis confirmed that diagnostic accuracy was an independent protective factor for the weakness of clinical transfer ability (HR = 0.6469, P &lt; 0.00001), meaning that students with higher diagnostic accuracy had a significantly superior clinical competence. Conclusions In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the teaching model combining AI-powered virtual simulation with real cases can comprehensively and significantly enhance the comprehensive clinical skills and learning experience of medical students. The teaching effect can effectively transfer to the real clinical environment, and the diagnostic accuracy cultivated during the teaching process has important predictive value for the long-term clinical prognosis. This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

analysis.methods: This study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in Clinical Medicine (five-year program) at China Three Gorges University. Teachers gave lectures combined with PPT demonstrations, supplemented by oral explanations of classic cases, and no virtual diagnosis and treatment platform operation was performed. The "Zhiqu" virtual clinical training platform (17) combined with CBL was adopted. The specific teaching process was as follows: (1) Pre-class preparation: The research team screened real emergency cases, which were entered into the Curefun platform after review by senior emergency physicians. Students previewed the case background through the platform before class, requiring a preview duration of no less than 30 min per case. (2) In-class teaching: Teachers guided students to discuss cases in groups. Students completed simulated operations such as medical history collection, auxiliary examination selection, diagnosis, and treatment plan formulation through the platform. The in-class platform operation duration was about 40 min per class hour, and teachers gave real-time comments and explanations on students' operation processes and results. (3) Post-class review: Students reviewed cases and completed extended case exercises through the platform, requiring a postclass platform usage duration of no less than 20 min per case. Meanwhile, the platform automatically recorded the cumulative usage duration of each student, the sub-item usage durations of pre-class preview, in-class operation, and post-class review, as well as the number of completed cases and the accuracy of diagnosis and treatment, which served as the core data for subsequent correlation analysis. Demographic data including gender, age, and place of origin (rural/urban) were collected via questionnaire. Before the initiation of the educational intervention, a baseline knowledge test (total score 100) consisting of multiple-choice questions, true/false questions, and short-answer questions was administered, and the scores were recorded. A unified final examination was conducted after course completion, consisting of objective items (multiple-choice and true/false questions, 40%) and case-analysis questions (60%), with a total score of 100. An objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) (18) assessment using standardized patients (SP) was organized at the end of the course. Assessment domains included history taking, physical examination, emergency skills, and doctorpatient communication. Scores were independently rated by two senior emergency physicians, and the mean score was adopted (total score 100). This domain included assessments of advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer effect. During the clinical internship in the emergency department, students' performance was evaluated by their supervising attending physicians. Advanced clinical competence was assessed across five subdomains: disease assessment (0-20 points), emergency management capability (0-30 points), clinical decision-making ability (0-20 points), interdisciplinary integration ability (0-20 points), and communication and teamwork (0-10 points), with a total score of 100. Clinical transfer effect was evaluated using the Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX) instrument (19). This included academic self-efficacy and self-directed learning ability. • The Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (ASES) was used to measure students' confidence in learning (20) . • The Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale (SDLRS) was used to assess autonomous learning ability (21, 22) . A self-designed questionnaire was used, covering six dimensions: satisfaction with the teaching model, improvement in clinical thinking ability, improvement in decision-making ability, improvement in emergency management ability, improvement in learning motivation, and improvement in knowledge mastery. A 5-point Likert scale was adopted (1 = strongly dissatisfied, 5 = strongly satisfied). Data were extracted from the platform's backend system, including six indicators: total usage duration, pre-class preparation duration, duration of in-class practice, post-class review duration, number of completed cases, and diagnostic accuracy, allowing precise recording of platform usage for each student. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (R version 4.3.1) and GraphPad Prism 9 software. Continuous data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (� x + s), and between-group comparisons were conducted using the independent-samples t-test. Categorical data were presented as number (percentage), and between-group differences were analyzed using the χ 2 -test. Statistical analyses were performed using appropriate parametric or nonparametric tests to compare baseline characteristics, academic performance, clinical competence, psychological scales, and questionnaire scores between the experimental and control groups. Stratified analyses were conducted in the experimental group according to Mini-CEX scores and diagnostic accuracy to explore differences in clinical performance and learning engagement among subgroups. Pearson or Spearman correlation analyses were used to evaluate the relationships among learning engagement, diagnostic accuracy, and clinical performance. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression models were applied to identify predictors and independent protective factors for the study outcome, with hazard ratios (HR), 95% confidence intervals (CI), and P-values reported. Subgroup analyses and interaction tests stratified by gender, region, baseline scores, and age were further performed to assess the robustness of the association between diagnostic accuracy and clinical outcomes. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

analysis.discussion: Emergency medicine poses unique pedagogical challenges for undergraduate medical students. Learners are required to rapidly integrate fragmented pre-clinical theoretical knowledge into practical clinical reasoning (23) . However, traditional teaching methods, such as theoretical lectures and limited clinical internships, have significant deficiencies in the dynamics and complexity of simulated emergency environments, making it difficult to effectively cultivate the high-level competencies of medical students, such as clinical decision-making, emergency handling, and teamwork (24, 25) . This weakness in ability cultivation directly affects the quality of the future medical workforce and may potentially increase the risk of medical errors. This study designed and implemented a randomized controlled trial to evaluate a new teaching model that integrates AI-powered virtual simulation technology with real emergency cases. Medical students were randomly divided into a control group receiving traditional teaching and an experimental group receiving the new teaching method. A multi-dimensional evaluation system was adopted, including theoretical assessment, OSCE, and clinical internship tracking assessment (such as Mini-CEX). Preliminary results suggest that the experimental group appears to demonstrate advantages in multiple evaluation dimensions. Compared with previous studies, the advantages of this study lie in its attempt to be among the first to integrate AI-driven virtual simulation platforms with structured real emergency cases and the use of a longitudinal, multi-dimensional evaluation system. This may help illustrate the potential superiority of this model in improving teaching effectiveness, more importantly, this study provides an early attempt, within emergency medicine education intervention research, to link objective skills assessment indicators (such as diagnostic accuracy) collected during teaching with long-term clinical internship performance and outcome risks. Although previous studies have explored the application of virtual simulation in nursing or specialized skills training (11, 13) and have focused on the development of specific courses for emergency resident physicians (23, 26) , there remains relatively limited evidence systematically assessing the impact of AI-powered virtual simulation combined with real cases on the full chain of medical students' theoretical knowledge, practical skills, and advanced clinical ability. Our results, that the experimental group outperformed the traditional teaching group in theoretical test, OSCE practical operation, advanced clinical abilities (such as emergency management, interdisciplinary integration), and learning satisfaction, offer preliminary empirical support for the potential effectiveness of this integration model. The findings of this study may yield several tentative practical implications for undergraduate emergency-medicine teaching. Firstly, the study suggests that the "AI-driven virtual simulation combined with real cases" teaching model can potentially compensate for the deficiencies of traditional teaching in the dynamics, complexity, and high-risk nature of simulated emergency environments. Differed from conventional lecturecentred teaching, which relies heavily on static textual and pictorial descriptions, the AI-driven virtual-simulation platform reconstructs dynamically-evolving emergency scenarios. It permits students to repeatedly practise under simulated time pressure, obtain immediate feedback on their diagnostic and therapeutic decisions, and conduct personalised repeated training. When combined with real-case-based learning, this approach reproduces the complex, high-risk decision-making context of emergency medicine within a safe pre-clinical setting, thereby potentially compensating for key deficiencies of traditional classroom-based teaching before students enter formal clinical rotations. These observations may provide preliminary evidence for medical schools and teaching hospitals to reform emergency medicine courses and introduce intelligent simulation teaching tools. Secondly, the study revealed that objective clinical skills, especially diagnostic accuracy, appeared to be independent protective factors for students' future clinical competence. This finding suggested that the medical education evaluation system may warrant consideration for reform, shifting from excessive emphasis on theoretical knowledge assessment to more emphasis and effective assessment of core clinical abilities closely related to patient safety and prognosis, such as through objective structured clinical examinations (OSCE) and diagnostic accuracy assessment to quantify students' practical competence (27) . Finally, according to students' selfreported questionnaire responses (subjective measurements), this teaching model appears to have improved students' learning interest, learning-related confidence and satisfaction with teaching. Complementary objective evidence for teaching effectiveness was obtained from examination results, clinical internship ratings and platform-usage records. Therefore, educational administrators may consider supporting the promotion and application of such student-centered, technology-enabled innovative teaching methods in course design and resource allocation. It is worth noting that, despite the educational merits of AIenhanced virtual simulation, gains in learning efficiency may come with notable potential costs for medical education: overreliance on standardised AI-generated scenarios could induce stereotyped clinical thinking and greater cognitive load, uneven access to AI educational resources risks widening the digital divide across institutions; and face-to-face faculty mentoring and interpersonal-skill training remain irreplaceable. Importantly, these pitfalls are not inherent to AI itself. In this study we mitigated these concerns by treating AI simulation only as a supplementary rather than replacement tool, integrating it with authentic case-based learning and emergency clinical rotations, capping task workload to reduce time burdens for learners and educators, and having all AI-generated cases manually checked by senior emergency physicians for clinical accuracy. While no adverse outcomes emerged in our short-term intervention, longer-term follow-up is still needed to uncover latent drawbacks and lasting effects of AI-integrated medical teaching. Of course, this study also has several limitations that need to be considered when interpreting the results and planning future research. First, the sample was derived from medical students in a single center and a single grade, and the sample size was relatively limited, which may restrict the generalizability of the research results to other institutions, students of different grades, or the resident physician group. Second, although clinical internship tracking and evaluation were conducted, the follow-up period might still not be sufficient to fully assess the long-term sustainability of the teaching effect and its ultimate impact on the career. Third, the study did not set up a control group of "only virtual simulation" or "only case teaching", so it was difficult to completely separate the respective contributions of the two teaching components. items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Marketing Strategies for Enhancing Sales Conversion in E-Commerce: An Empirical and Analytical Investigation

items.abstract_text: The rapid expansion of global e-commerce has intensified competition for consumer attention, rendering traditional demographic-segmented and rule-based marketing increasingly ineffective. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in digital marketing, enabling firms to process high-velocity behavioral datasets and deliver hyper-personalized customer journeys in real time. While industry adoption of AI marketing tools is widespread, a substantial maturity gap persists between experimental deployment and fully scaled conversion optimization. This paper integrates a multi-stage analytical research design—combining psychometric Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) of consumer survey data ($N = 420$), econometric before-and-after funnel cohort modeling across retail deployments, and regression-based moderation analysis—to quantify how AI-enabled digital marketing drives sales conversion. Specifically, the study examines four core strategic pillars: neural recommendation engines, predictive programmatic acquisition, dynamic pricing optimization, and generative conversational AI. Analytical results demonstrate that Perceived Personalization significantly enhances Customer Experience Quality ($\beta = 0.499, p < 0.001$) and Digital Marketing Effectiveness ($\beta = 0.488, p < 0.001$), which jointly mediate downstream Purchase Intention and actual checkout conversion ($R^2 = 0.412$). Econometric cohort tracking further reveals a 23.4% to 31.0% relative lift in session-to-purchase conversion rates, a 27% reduction in bounce rates, and up to a 50% increase in Average Order Value (AOV) via real-time affinity bundling. However, moderation analysis confirms that perceived algorithmic opacity and privacy intrusion negatively attenuate conversion gains ($\beta = -0.214, p < 0.01$). The study concludes with an actionable governance and MLOps framework for balancing algorithmic conversion efficiency with consumer trust.
